meta.blurb: A rich king asks a wise visitor who the happiest man is, expecting to hear his own name. The answer is a warning. Herodotus follows kings and oracles to the Persian wars, with Marathon, a bridge of boats and three hundred Spartans.
meta.bible: Herodotus: the Greek writer from Halicarnassus who gathered the stories; he calls his work an inquiry; he often says what he was told and lets the reader decide. Halicarnassus: his home city on the coast of Asia Minor. Croesus: the rich king of Lydia, whose capital is Sardis. Solon: the wise Athenian who visits Croesus. Tellus: an Athenian Solon names as happy. Cleobis and Biton: two brothers who pulled their mother's cart to a temple. Delphi: the temple of Apollo where the Oracle speaks. Oracle: the priestess of Delphi, whose answers are riddles. Cyrus: the founder of the Persian Empire. Astyages: the king of the Medes, Cyrus's grandfather. Harpagus: Astyages's officer. Mitradates: the herdsman who saves baby Cyrus. Tomyris: queen of the Massagetae. Cambyses: Cyrus's son, who conquers Egypt. Darius: the king who follows Cambyses. Xerxes: Darius's son. Psammetichus: an Egyptian king. Khufu: the Egyptian king who built the great pyramid. Polycrates: the lucky tyrant of Samos. Smerdis: the false king who is killed by seven nobles. Mardonius: a Persian general. Artabanus: Xerxes's wise uncle. Demaratus: an exiled Spartan king who advises Xerxes. Datis and Artaphernes: the Persian commanders at Marathon. Miltiades: the Athenian general at Marathon. Pheidippides: the Athenian runner. Pan: the goat-footed god. Themistocles: the Athenian leader who builds a fleet. Leonidas: the king of Sparta at Thermopylae. Ephialtes: the traitor who shows the Persians a path. Artemisia: the queen of Halicarnassus who fights for Xerxes. Pausanias: the Spartan commander at Plataea. Persians: the people of the great Persian Empire, led by their king. Greeks: the people of the many small Greek cities. Medes: the people who ruled before the Persians. Lydians: the people of Lydia. Egyptians: the people of Egypt. Scythians: the nomads of the northern plains. Spartans: the soldiers of Sparta. Athenians: the people of Athens. Immortals: the Persian king's ten thousand chosen soldiers. Empire: a land of many peoples under one ruler. Pyre: a pile of wood for burning. Satrap: a governor of a Persian province. Herald: a messenger. Tyrant: a ruler who took power by himself. Persia, Lydia, Sardis, Babylon, Egypt, the Nile, Athens, Sparta, Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, Plataea, Mycale, Sestos, the Hellespont, Mount Athos, Samos, Miletus, Eretria, Lade, Artemisium, Ionia, the Euphrates, the Halys, Pteria, Doriscus: the places. Dates are about: Cyrus takes Sardis about 546 BC, Babylon in 539 BC, Cambyses takes Egypt in 525 BC, Darius becomes king in 522 BC, Marathon is 490 BC, Thermopylae and Salamis 480 BC, Plataea and Mycale 479 BC. Voice and tone: a curious, warm storyteller; he says 'they say' when he is not sure; his numbers are often too big and the text says so; wars are told without gore. Added for the full-length book (200 beats in 20 chapters of ten, ending with Cyrus's warning). People of the old tales: Io: a princess of Argos carried off in the Persian version. Europa: a Phoenician princess. Medea: a princess of Colchis. Paris: the Trojan prince who takes Helen. Helen: in the Egyptian priests' story she waits in Egypt under Proteus. Priam: king of Troy. Proteus: a king of Egypt in the priests' story. Phoenicians: sea traders; Phoenician ships fill the Persian fleet. Lydia: Croesus's kingdom, capital Sardis; Lydians struck the first gold and silver coins. Candaules: the Lydian king killed by Gyges. Gyges: his guard, who becomes king; the Oracle says vengeance will fall on his fifth descendant, Croesus. Bias and Pittacus: wise Greeks of Priene and Mytilene. Arion: the singer saved by a dolphin; Periander: the tyrant of Corinth. Solon's visit to Sardis: Tellus, Cleobis and Biton are named as happy; Hera: the goddess whose priestess is their mother; Argos: their city. Atys: Croesus's son, killed by Adrastus, a Phrygian exile, in a boar hunt in Mysia. Croesus had a second son who could not speak. Cyrus's birth: Astyages dreams of Mandane, his daughter, and marries her to Cambyses, a Persian. Harpagus is told to kill the baby; Mitradates the herdsman and his wife swap the baby for their own stillborn child. Artembares: a Median noble whose son Cyrus has whipped. Cyrus overthrows Astyages about 550 BC. Croesus tests seven oracles; Delphi answers; Sandanis warns him; Pteria is fought to a draw; the Lydian horses flee from camels; Sardis falls about 546 BC through a cliff path found by Hyroeades. Croesus's mute son speaks. Cyrus's pyre: Croesus cries out Solon's name. The Phocaeans sink a lump of iron and sail away. Babylon: taken in 539 BC by turning the Euphrates aside. The Gyndes: the river Cyrus splits into 360 channels. Tomyris: queen of the Massagetae; her son Spargapises; Cyrus dreams that Darius, son of Hystaspes, has wings; he dies about 530 BC after 29 years. Egypt: Amasis, a commoner, becomes king after Apries; Psammenitus is his son and reigns six months; Psammetichus tests the oldest people with two babies; Hecataeus is shown 345 statues at Thebes; the Egyptian year has twelve months of thirty days and five more; Rhampsinitus: a king whose treasury is robbed; Bubastis: the festival town; Naucratis: the Greek trading town. Cambyses invades in 525 BC: Phanes of Halicarnassus defects; the skulls at Pelusium; the Apis bull; the lost army of fifty thousand; the Ethiopian bow. Polycrates of Samos throws his emerald ring into the sea; Oroetes tricks him. Cambyses dies about 522 BC; Prexaspes killed Smerdis in secret; the false Smerdis is a Magus without ears; Phaedymia is Otanes's daughter. The seven: Otanes, Aspathines, Gobryas, Hydarnes, Megabyzus, Intaphrenes and Darius; Oebares is Darius's groom; Democedes of Croton: the Greek doctor. Darius makes twenty provinces and the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa. Scythians: their king Idanthyrsus; Targitaus: their first king in their story; Mandrocles of Samos bridges the Bosporus; Darius crosses the Danube (the Ister) about 513 BC; Nasamonians cross the Libyan desert; Necho: the Egyptian king whose sailors go round Africa; Scylax of Caryanda explores the Indus. Athens: Hippias and Hipparchus are sons of Peisistratus; Harmodius and Aristogeiton kill Hipparchus in 514 BC; Hippias is expelled in 510 BC; Cleisthenes makes the democracy; Cleomenes: king of Sparta, and his daughter Gorgo; Aristagoras: ruler of Miletus, begins the Ionian revolt in 499 BC; Histiaeus: sends a message tattooed under a slave's hair; Sardis burns in 498 BC; Dionysius of Phocaea trains the fleet at Lade in 494 BC; Phrynichus: the playwright fined for his play on the fall of Miletus; Artaphernes: the Persian governor at Sardis. Mardonius loses his fleet at Mount Athos in 492 BC. Darius asks for earth and water in 491 BC; heralds are thrown into a pit at Athens and a well at Sparta. Miltiades: son of Cimon, ruled the Chersonese, later fails at Paros; Datis spares Delos; Eretria falls after six days; Hippias loses a tooth at Marathon; Callimachus: the Athenian war leader, killed at Marathon; Cynegirus and Epizelus: Athenians in the battle; Stesilaus: an Athenian general killed at Marathon; Plataeans help at Marathon; Darius dies in 486 BC after 36 years. Xerxes marches in 480 BC; Artabanus: his uncle; the Hellespont bridges of 674 ships (360 and 314); Pythius the Lydian: the rich host at Sardis; Abydos: where Xerxes weeps; Doriscus: where the army is counted; Artemisia: queen of Halicarnassus, five ships. Gelon: ruler of Syracuse. Eurybiades: Spartan admiral. Adeimantus: Corinthian commander. Sperthias and Bulis: Spartans who go to Xerxes. Dieneces: Spartan who jokes about arrows hiding the sun. Megistias: the seer. Hydarnes leads the Immortals over the mountain. Aristodemus: Spartan called the Trembler, who dies bravely at Plataea. Aristides the Just: Athenian; Sicinnus: Themistocles's servant; Ameinias: the Athenian who rams first at Salamis; Salamis falls in late September 480 BC. Alexander: king of Macedon. Plataea 479 BC: Chileus of Tegea persuades Sparta; Amompharetus: the Spartan with the stone; Masistius: Persian cavalry leader; Arimnestus: the Spartan who kills Mardonius; Artabazus: Persian who flees with forty thousand; Attaginus: the Theban host; Thersander of Orchomenus: the Greek guest who heard the Persian speak. Mycale 479 BC: Leotychides: Spartan king; Hegesistratus of Samos. Sestos: Artayctes governs; Protesilaus: the hero whose shrine he robbed; Xanthippus: the Athenian commander. Places: Abdera, Acropolis, Aegean, Aegina, Africa, Aigaleos, Ammon, Araxes, Arcadia, Attica, Boeotia, Bosporus, Byzantium, Caspian, Chersonese, Chios, Cilicia, Cithaeron, Corcyra, Crete, Croton, Cyprus, Danube, Delos, Ecbatana, Elephantine, Ethiopia, Euboea, Europe, Gargaphia, Heliopolis, Indus, India, Isthmus, Istanbul, Labyrinth, Laurium, Libya, Macedon, Macedonia, Magnesia, Mantinea, Memphis, Moeris, Mycenae, Mysia, Niger, Olympus, Orchomenus, Parnassus, Paros, Pelusium, Peloponnese, Phalerum, Phrygia, Psyttaleia, Siwa, Sunium, Susa, Syracuse, Syria, Tegea, Tempe, Tenos, Thasos, Thebes, Thespiae, Thessaly, Thrace, Troezen. Peoples: Arabs, Arcadians, Callatian Indians, Chians, Cypriots, Delphians, Eretrians, Ethiopians, Euboeans, Lesbians, Locrians, Magi, Magus, Medians, Megarians, Nasamonians, Phocians, Samians, Sidonians, Tegeans, Thebans, Thespians, Thessalians, Zeus: the chief god, Athena, Artemis, Apollo, Boreas, Cybele and Heracles: gods and heroes. The Oracle says things in riddles. Dates are about: Hippias leaves 510 BC, the Ionian revolt 499 to 494 BC, Lade and Miletus 494 BC, Athos 492 BC, Marathon 490 BC, Xerxes crosses the Hellespont 480 BC.

beats.scene: Herodotus writes on a scroll at a desk beside the sea
beats.summary: Herodotus opens his inquiry so that great deeds will not be forgotten.

beats.scene: A Phoenician ship at a Greek harbour with women on the beach
beats.summary: Persian storytellers say Phoenicians stole Io, and that Greeks then stole Europa and Medea in return.

beats.scene: Greek ships crowd a beach below the walls of Troy
beats.summary: Paris takes Helen, the Greeks sail to Troy, and the Persians say that this was the real beginning of their hatred.

beats.scene: Herodotus counts cities on a tablet while ships sail past
beats.summary: Herodotus will not decide who began the quarrel, and will name the first man he knows wronged the Greeks, adding that fortune never stays in one place.

beats.scene: Candaules and a guard stand in a royal bedroom at Sardis
beats.summary: Croesus's ancestor, King Candaules of Lydia, boasts of his wife's beauty and forces his guard Gyges to look at her.

beats.scene: Gyges stands in a doorway as the queen turns and sees him
beats.summary: The queen notices Gyges, and gives him the choice between dying and killing the king, and Gyges becomes king.

beats.scene: Croesus on horseback in front of the walls of a Greek city
beats.summary: Croesus conquers the Greek cities of Asia, beginning with Ephesus, and makes them pay him tribute.

beats.scene: Croesus listens to a wise Greek beside a half-built ship
beats.summary: Croesus plans a fleet to attack the islands, but a wise Greek warns him that islanders would welcome a battle at sea.

beats.scene: Lydians play dice on a hillside while others bake bread
beats.summary: The Lydians are the first to use gold and silver coins, and they invented games to survive a famine.

beats.scene: A dolphin carries a singing man across the waves at sunset
beats.summary: A singer named Arion, thrown overboard by sailors who wanted his money, is carried to shore by a dolphin.

beats.scene: Solon the Athenian walks into the golden city of Sardis
beats.summary: Solon gives Athens its laws, leaves for ten years to travel, and arrives at the court of Croesus.

beats.scene: Servants show Solon chests of gold and jewels in the treasury
beats.summary: Croesus has his servants show Solon every treasure, and then asks him who is the happiest man he has ever seen.

beats.scene: An Athenian soldier lies on a battlefield at sunset as friends gather
beats.summary: Solon names Tellus of Athens, who had a rich city, fine sons and grandchildren, and died bravely in battle.

beats.scene: Two young men pull an ox cart to a temple, then sleep in it
beats.summary: Solon names Cleobis and Biton, brothers who pulled their mother's cart to the temple of Hera and then died peacefully in their sleep.

beats.scene: Croesus frowns on his golden throne as Solon speaks calmly
beats.summary: Croesus is angry, and Solon explains that life is long, that no two days are alike, and that only the end shows whether a man was happy.

beats.scene: Croesus asleep with a worried face while a dark shape stands over him
beats.summary: Croesus sends Solon away as a fool, and soon dreams that his son Atys will die by an iron spear.

beats.scene: A young man in a palace room where spears are being carried out
beats.summary: Croesus finds Atys a wife, keeps him from war, and removes the spears from the palace, while a stranger named Adrastus arrives.

beats.scene: A huge boar rushes out of the forest above a Mysian village
beats.summary: A boar ruins the fields of Mysia, and Croesus sends hunters but keeps Atys at home until Atys argues him round and Adrastus is sent as guard.

beats.scene: A hunter's spear flies toward a boar as a young man falls
beats.summary: In the hunt, Adrastus's spear misses the boar and strikes Atys, so the dream comes true.

beats.scene: Croesus kneels beside his son's body as Adrastus stands silent
beats.summary: Croesus mourns Atys and forgives Adrastus, but Adrastus takes his own life at the tomb.

beats.scene: A king wakes in the night in a Median palace with a worried face
beats.summary: Astyages, king of the Medes, dreams that his daughter Mandane floods all of Asia, and marries her to a Persian named Cambyses.

beats.scene: A green vine grows from a young woman's side and covers a land
beats.summary: A second dream, of a vine from Mandane that covers Asia, makes Astyages order Harpagus to kill her newborn son.

beats.scene: A herdsman and his wife swap two babies in a mountain hut
beats.summary: Harpagus passes the order to the herdsman Mitradates, but the herdsman and his wife swap the baby for their own stillborn child.

beats.scene: Boys play kings in a village while one stands in a crown of leaves
beats.summary: At ten, Cyrus is chosen as king in a children's game, and orders the other boys about.

beats.scene: A king looks closely at a boy who stands bravely before him
beats.summary: Cyrus has a nobleman's son beaten for disobeying, and the angry father brings him before Astyages, who sees a family likeness.

beats.scene: A herdsman kneels before an angry king in a stone hall
beats.summary: Mitradates confesses the truth, and Astyages pretends to forgive him, but sends Cyrus away to Persia.

beats.scene: Harpagus stands alone in a dark hall after a feast
beats.summary: Astyages punishes Harpagus by killing his son, and Harpagus hides his anger and bows.

beats.scene: A hunter cuts open a hare beside a mountain track
beats.summary: Harpagus sends Cyrus a secret letter hidden inside the body of a hare, urging him to rise against Astyages.

beats.scene: Persian men clear a field of thorns, then eat at a great feast
beats.summary: Cyrus has the Persians clear a thorny field for a day and feast on the next, to show them the choice between toil and ease.

beats.scene: Median soldiers throw down their spears as a tall officer turns away
beats.summary: In the war that follows, Harpagus and many Medes desert, and Astyages loses to Cyrus.

beats.scene: Messengers on horseback leave Sardis for seven famous oracles
beats.summary: Croesus fears Cyrus and sends messengers to test the oracles, and only Delphi guesses that he is cooking a tortoise and a lamb.

beats.scene: A golden lion stands on a stack of gold bars in a sunlit temple
beats.summary: Croesus gives Delphi huge sacrifices and gifts of gold, and then puts his question about Persia.

beats.scene: A priestess sits on a stool above smoke in a mountain temple
beats.summary: The oracle tells Croesus that if he crosses the Halys, a great empire will fall, and that he should beware when a mule rules the Medes.

beats.scene: A tall woman in armour rides in a chariot into Athens
beats.summary: Croesus asks which Greeks are strongest and hears of Sparta and Athens, and Herodotus tells how Peisistratus tricked Athens into accepting him as tyrant.

beats.scene: A wise old Lydian speaks seriously to Croesus on his throne
beats.summary: A Lydian named Sandanis warns Croesus that the Persians are a hard people with nothing worth taking, but Croesus ignores him.

beats.scene: Soldiers cross a wide river on foot behind a king on horseback
beats.summary: Croesus crosses the Halys, and fights a hard battle at Pteria that no one wins.

beats.scene: Croesus rides home at night past empty fields toward Sardis
beats.summary: Croesus goes home to Sardis, sends his hired soldiers away for the winter, and hopes to bring his allies together in the spring.

beats.scene: Lydian horsemen rear in panic as a line of camels advances
beats.summary: Cyrus meets the Lydian cavalry outside Sardis with a line of camels at the front, and their horses panic.

beats.scene: A soldier climbs a steep rock face at night toward a quiet wall
beats.summary: Cyrus besieges Sardis for fourteen days, and a Persian soldier sees a Lydian guard retrieve a dropped helmet and learns a way up the cliff.

beats.scene: A mute young man shouts at a soldier raising his spear over a king
beats.summary: A Persian soldier almost kills Croesus without knowing who he is, but his son, who had never spoken, cries out to stop him.

beats.scene: Croesus stands in chains on a pyre as rain clouds gather
beats.summary: Cyrus puts Croesus on a pyre, but at the name of Solon he relents, and a storm sent after Croesus prays to Apollo puts out the fire.

beats.scene: Croesus holds an iron chain beside the priestess of Delphi
beats.summary: Croesus sends his chains to Delphi and complains, and the oracle answers that he misunderstood the words about the empire and the mule.

beats.scene: A piper plays by the sea while fish ignore him on the sand
beats.summary: The Ionian Greeks ask Cyrus for terms, and he tells them the fable of the piper and the fish, while a Spartan herald warns him to leave the Greeks alone.

beats.scene: A ship full of families sails away as a blazing lump of iron sinks
beats.summary: Harpagus conquers the Ionian cities, but the people of Phocaea sail away, swearing not to return until a lump of iron floats.

beats.scene: Persian boys practise riding and shooting arrows on open ground
beats.summary: Herodotus describes the Persians: no temples, feasts with wine, and boys taught to ride, shoot and tell the truth.

beats.scene: A great river runs through a vast walled city with bronze gates
beats.summary: Cyrus marches against Babylon, wasting a year over the river Gyndes, and arrives at a vast city with walls as wide as a chariot road.

beats.scene: Persian soldiers wade along a dried river bed toward the walls of Babylon
beats.summary: Cyrus takes Babylon in 539 BC by turning the Euphrates aside and entering along the river bed while the city is feasting.

beats.scene: A queen in plain dress speaks calmly to a Persian messenger by a river
beats.summary: Cyrus marches against Queen Tomyris of the Massagetae, and Croesus advises him to cross the river Araxes and set a trap.

beats.scene: A Persian camp with a feast laid out beside sleeping soldiers
beats.summary: Cyrus dreams that Darius has wings that cover Asia and Europe, and sets a trap of food and wine for the Massagetae.

beats.scene: Queen Tomyris stands before her army on a grassy plain
beats.summary: Tomyris defeats Cyrus in a great battle, and the king dies about 530 BC after twenty-nine years on the throne.

beats.scene: A wide river in flood flows past green fields beside the desert
beats.summary: Cyrus's son Cambyses plans to invade Egypt, and Herodotus describes Egypt as the gift of the Nile and its yearly flood.

beats.scene: An Egyptian woman sells goods at a market stall while a man weaves
beats.summary: Herodotus finds that Egyptian customs are the opposite of Greek ones, with women in the market and men at the loom.

beats.scene: Egyptian priests walk past a temple where cats sit in the sun
beats.summary: Herodotus notes how deeply the Egyptians respect their sacred animals, especially cats, and how they grieve when one dies.

beats.scene: Two babies lie on straw in a quiet hut while a shepherd listens
beats.summary: King Psammetichus tests which people are the oldest by raising two babies in silence, and the first word they say sounds like a Phrygian one.

beats.scene: A boat sails up a wide river past desert cliffs and green banks
beats.summary: Herodotus asks about the sources of the Nile, but no one can say, so he considers the answers of Greek thinkers.

beats.scene: A crocodile lies on a muddy bank while a small bird picks its teeth
beats.summary: Herodotus describes crocodiles, hippopotamuses and the little bird that is said to clean a crocodile's teeth.

beats.scene: Priests wrap a body in white linen beside a table of salt
beats.summary: Herodotus describes embalming in three grades, and the custom of showing a carved mummy at feasts to remind the guests that life is short.

beats.scene: Thousands of workers drag huge stones toward a growing pyramid
beats.summary: King Khufu builds the great pyramid, and Herodotus tells of the workers, and of the hatred the Egyptians felt for the king.

beats.scene: A thief hides in a dark stone room beside a heap of treasure
beats.summary: Herodotus tells how thieves rob the treasury of King Rhampsinitus, and how the cleverest of them wins the king's daughter.

beats.scene: A vast stone building with endless corridors and courtyards stands by a lake
beats.summary: Herodotus visits the Labyrinth near Lake Moeris, which he thinks more wonderful than the pyramids.

beats.scene: A priest shows a Greek visitor rows of wooden statues in a hall
beats.summary: Priests at Thebes show the Greek writer Hecataeus 345 statues of high priests, to prove that Egypt's past is far older than any Greek family tree.

beats.scene: Priests count days on a stone calendar as the sun rises
beats.summary: Herodotus explains that the Egyptians were the first to divide the year into twelve months of thirty days, with five days added at the end.

beats.scene: Priests tell Herodotus a story in a temple courtyard
beats.summary: The priests tell Herodotus that Paris and Helen were driven to Egypt by a storm, where King Proteus sent Paris away and kept Helen safe.

beats.scene: Greek soldiers outside Troy argue with Trojans on the walls
beats.summary: Herodotus argues that the priests are right, because the Trojans would have given Helen back rather than lose their city, and he believes that the gods wished to show that great wrongs bring great punishments.

beats.scene: A common soldier is lifted up by a crowd and given a helmet
beats.summary: Amasis, a commoner, is crowned king of Egypt by rebels, and the Egyptians at first despise him.

beats.scene: Servants melt down a golden basin while Amasis watches calmly
beats.summary: Amasis melts a golden footbath into a statue of a god, and then uses it to teach the Egyptians that his rank is as new as the statue.

beats.scene: Amasis laughs with friends at a table in the evening
beats.summary: Amasis works all morning and drinks and jokes in the afternoon, and tells his critics that a bow kept always bent would break.

beats.scene: Boats full of singing people drift down a river to a festival
beats.summary: Herodotus describes the great festival at Bubastis, where thousands of people sail to the temple, singing and playing music.

beats.scene: Greek merchants unload ships at a busy riverside market town
beats.summary: Amasis gives the Greeks the trading town of Naucratis, and Herodotus says that many Greek gods have Egyptian names.

beats.scene: A glowing bird carries a large egg toward a temple of the sun
beats.summary: Herodotus describes the phoenix and says that he does not quite believe the tale, then ends his account of Egypt as the land of the most wonders.

beats.scene: A Greek soldier speaks with an Arab chief beside a line of camels
beats.summary: A Greek officer, Phanes, leaves the Egyptian king and helps Cambyses cross the desert with water carried on camels.

beats.scene: Skulls of two kinds lie scattered on a sandy battlefield
beats.summary: At Pelusium in 525 BC the Persians beat the Egyptians, and Herodotus later sees the bones and finds Persian skulls thin and Egyptian skulls thick.

beats.scene: A captive king watches silently as a line of prisoners walks by
beats.summary: Cambyses tests the defeated Psammenitus, who does not weep at his own children's sorrow but weeps for an old friend.

beats.scene: Persian scouts approach a pale king beside a great bow
beats.summary: Cambyses sends spies to Ethiopia, whose king answers with a bow too large for Persian arms.

beats.scene: A long line of soldiers walks into a rising wall of sand
beats.summary: Cambyses sends fifty thousand men against the oracle of Ammon, and they disappear in the desert and are never seen again.

beats.scene: A king in Persian dress stands over a wounded sacred bull
beats.summary: Cambyses stabs the sacred Apis bull and mocks Egyptian customs, and Herodotus concludes that he has gone mad.

beats.scene: A king dreams in bed while a messenger holds a young man's hand
beats.summary: Cambyses dreams that his brother Smerdis will take his throne, and he sends a trusted servant to kill him in secret.

beats.scene: Polycrates and his captains stand on a harbour wall above a fleet
beats.summary: Polycrates seizes power in Samos, builds a great fleet and, Herodotus says, three of the greatest works in Greece.

beats.scene: A gold ring falls from a boat into the dark sea
beats.summary: Polycrates throws away his favourite ring to test his luck, and a few days later a fisherman brings it back inside a fish.

beats.scene: A man in a purple cloak walks into a harbour town alone
beats.summary: Amasis breaks with Polycrates, who is lured to the mainland by a Persian governor with promises of gold and meets a sad end.

beats.scene: A king lies wounded in a tent as his generals bend over him
beats.summary: Cambyses hears that a false Smerdis has taken his throne, wounds himself with his own sword as he mounts his horse, and dies about 522 BC.

beats.scene: A man looks closely at a tall figure whose hair hides his ears
beats.summary: Otanes suspects that the new king is a fraud, and learns from his daughter, one of the king's wives, that the king has no ears.

beats.scene: Seven men in cloaks stand in a circle in a quiet garden
beats.summary: Otanes gathers other nobles, and Darius joins them and urges them to act at once.

beats.scene: Seven nobles run through a dark palace corridor with daggers
beats.summary: The seven kill the false king and his brother, and the Persians, angry at the Magi, drive them out.

beats.scene: Three nobles speak in turn at a table in a candlelit hall
beats.summary: The conspirators debate what kind of government Persia should have: rule by the many, by a few, or by one man.

beats.scene: Seven horsemen wait at dawn outside a city gate
beats.summary: The seven agree that the first man whose horse neighs at sunrise will be king, and Darius's groom arranges a trick that makes his master win.

beats.scene: Darius on a throne wearing a crown, with six nobles bowing
beats.summary: Darius becomes king in 522 BC and the others bow, and later a Greek doctor named Democedes cures the king's twisted ankle and is richly rewarded.

beats.scene: Persian officials count sacks of silver and gold dust at a long table
beats.summary: Darius divides the empire into twenty provinces, each with its own governor and its own fixed tax, and the Persians call him the shopkeeper.

beats.scene: A rider hands a message to a fresh rider at a roadside station
beats.summary: Darius keeps the Royal Road with stations for fresh riders, so that messages travel faster than anything else on land.

beats.scene: Greek and Indian men stand before Darius while an interpreter speaks
beats.summary: Darius asks Greeks and Indians to do something that breaks their customs, and Herodotus concludes that custom is king of all.

beats.scene: Golden tools fall from the sky onto a grassy plain
beats.summary: Darius plans to punish the Scythians, and Herodotus tells how they say the first Scythian king was born, and how golden gifts fell from the sky.

beats.scene: Scythian families live in wagons on the open grassland
beats.summary: The Scythians have no cities or farms to defend, and live in wagons on their herds, which makes them almost impossible to conquer.

beats.scene: A bridge of boats stretches across a wide muddy river
beats.summary: Darius crosses the Bosporus by a bridge built by a Greek engineer, then crosses the Danube on a bridge of boats built by Ionian Greeks.

beats.scene: A bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows lie before a king
beats.summary: The Scythians send Darius a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows, and the Persians disagree about what the gifts mean.

beats.scene: Scythian horsemen ride away across a wide empty plain
beats.summary: The Scythians retreat before Darius, drive off their cattle and fill the wells, and their king answers with a defiant message.

beats.scene: Scythian horsemen chase a hare across the plain as armies face each other
beats.summary: When the armies face each other, a hare runs between them and the Scythians chase it, which shows Darius how little they think of him.

beats.scene: Donkeys bray in an empty Persian camp as horsemen ride away
beats.summary: Darius slips away at night leaving his sick men and the donkeys behind, and the Scythians race to the bridge, but the Ionian tyrants keep their promise.

beats.scene: Five young men walk across a hot desert toward a distant green tree
beats.summary: Herodotus tells how five young men of the Nasamonian people cross the desert of Libya and find a river with crocodiles beyond it.

beats.scene: A Phoenician ship sails around a coast with the sun on its right
beats.summary: King Necho of Egypt sends Phoenician sailors round Africa, and Herodotus does not believe their report that the sun was on their right.

beats.scene: A ship sails down a wide river toward the sea in a far land
beats.summary: Darius sends a Greek captain named Scylax to explore the river Indus, and adds the Indus lands to his empire.

beats.scene: Two men with hidden daggers wait in a crowded Athenian street
beats.summary: Two friends, Harmodius and Aristogeiton, kill the tyrant Hipparchus in 514 BC, but his brother Hippias rules on more harshly.

beats.scene: A priestess at Delphi speaks to Spartan envoys in a hushed temple
beats.summary: The Alcmaeonids persuade the oracle to tell Sparta to free Athens, and in 510 BC the Spartans drive Hippias out.

beats.scene: Athenian citizens raise their hands to vote in an open square
beats.summary: Cleisthenes gives Athens a new government in which all citizens have a voice, and Herodotus says that this made the Athenians strong.

beats.scene: A Spartan king looks at a bronze map held by a visitor
beats.summary: Aristagoras of Miletus asks Sparta to help the Ionians, but gives up when he learns that Susa is three months' journey from the sea.

beats.scene: A stranger speaks to a huge crowd of Athenians in the open air
beats.summary: Aristagoras goes to Athens, where thirty thousand citizens agree to send twenty ships, which Herodotus calls the beginning of troubles.

beats.scene: A slave sits patiently while a man writes on his shaved head
beats.summary: Histiaeus, who is held at Susa, sends a secret message to Aristagoras by shaving a slave's head and writing on it, and waits for the hair to grow back.

beats.scene: Greek citizens throw down a tyrant's statue in a city square
beats.summary: Aristagoras gives up his own power, and the Ionian cities turn out their tyrants and choose their own leaders.

beats.scene: Flames spread over the reed roofs of a city on a hill
beats.summary: In 498 BC the Greeks burn Sardis, including the temple of the goddess Cybele, and then retreat with the Persians behind them.

beats.scene: A servant whispers to a king at dinner; an arrow flies skyward
beats.summary: Darius asks who the Athenians are, shoots an arrow into the sky and orders a servant to remind him three times at every dinner.

beats.scene: Persian soldiers chase retreating Greeks through a wooded valley by a river
beats.summary: The Persians catch the Greeks near Ephesus and win, and Athens takes its ships home, though the revolt goes on.

beats.scene: Greek ships and Phoenician ships crowd together in a sunlit bay
beats.summary: A great Persian fleet gathers to crush the revolt, and the Ionians assemble their ships at the island of Lade.

beats.scene: Greek sailors row hard in rows while a captain shouts orders
beats.summary: Dionysius of Phocaea drills the Ionian fleet for a week, but the Ionians refuse to work so hard, and at Lade the Samians sail away.

beats.scene: A burning city by the sea with people looking back from ships
beats.summary: Miletus falls in 494 BC, and the Athenians are so moved by a play about its fall that they fine the writer and forbid the play.

beats.scene: A Persian officer measures land with a rope beside Greek farmers
beats.summary: The Persians settle peace in Ionia, measure the land fairly, fix taxes and, Herodotus says, set up democracies in the Ionian cities.

beats.scene: Great waves break ships against steep rocks beneath a high mountain
beats.summary: A Persian fleet is wrecked in a storm off Mount Athos in 492 BC, with the loss of three hundred ships and about twenty thousand men.

beats.scene: Persian heralds stand at the edge of a deep pit and a well
beats.summary: Darius demands earth and water from the Greek cities, and Athens and Sparta throw his heralds into a pit and a well.

beats.scene: Miltiades stands in an Athenian court while citizens listen
beats.summary: Miltiades, who knows the Persians well from his years in the Chersonese, returns to Athens and is elected a general.

beats.scene: Persian ships sail past an island as smoke rises from an altar
beats.summary: The Persian fleet of Datis and Artaphernes sails in 490 BC and spares the holy island of Delos, burning incense on the altar.

beats.scene: Persian soldiers enter an Athenian colony as citizens look on
beats.summary: Eretria resists for six days, but is betrayed to the Persians, who burn its temples and carry off its people.

beats.scene: An old man sneezes on a beach as soldiers land from ships
beats.summary: Hippias guides the Persians to the plain of Marathon, and he loses a tooth in the sand, taking it as a sign that he will never win back his city.

beats.scene: Pheidippides runs along a mountain path as a goat-footed god appears
beats.summary: Pheidippides runs to Sparta for help, meets the god Pan on the way, and hears that the Spartans must wait for the full moon.

beats.scene: Ten Athenian generals argue around a table while a leader stands
beats.summary: The ten Athenian generals are split five to five, and Miltiades persuades the war leader Callimachus to cast the deciding vote for battle.

beats.scene: Plataean soldiers arrive at an Athenian camp on a hot morning
beats.summary: The Plataeans arrive to help, and Miltiades, who holds back until his own day of command, plans his battle line.

beats.scene: Athenian soldiers charge downhill at a run toward Persian lines
beats.summary: Miltiades leads the Athenians in a charge at the run across the plain, which Herodotus says the Greeks had never done before.

beats.scene: Persian ships sail away from the shore as Athenian soldiers cheer
beats.summary: The Athenian wings defeat the Persians, then turn to help the weak centre, and the invaders flee to their ships.

beats.scene: An Athenian soldier reaches for a ship as a wounded man falls
beats.summary: Callimachus dies in the battle, and Herodotus tells of other brave men, including Cynegirus, who lost a hand holding a ship, and Epizelus, who lost his sight.

beats.scene: A shield flashes on a distant hill as ships turn toward Sunium
beats.summary: A shield is seen flashing a signal, and the Persian fleet sails for Athens, but the Athenian army marches home in time and the Persians go away.

beats.scene: Spartan soldiers walk across a plain of fallen Persian soldiers
beats.summary: Two thousand Spartans arrive on the next day, look at the dead Persians and praise the Athenians for their victory.

beats.scene: A wounded general is carried before a hostile Athenian court
beats.summary: Miltiades tries to take the island of Paros, fails, and dies of his wound, but the Athenians never forget what he did at Marathon.

beats.scene: Darius sits on his throne in anger above a map of the Greek lands
beats.summary: Darius, angry at the defeat, prepares a greater army, but dies in 486 BC, and his son Xerxes becomes king.

beats.scene: A young king rests his hand on a map beside two advisers
beats.summary: The new king Xerxes is reluctant to attack Greece, but his cousin Mardonius presses him to go and punish Athens.

beats.scene: Persian nobles sit in a great hall while one old man stands to speak
beats.summary: Xerxes tells his council that he will conquer Greece, and his wise uncle Artabanus warns him that the land and sea will be his greatest enemies.

beats.scene: A tall bright figure stands over a sleeping king in the dark
beats.summary: Xerxes dreams that a figure orders him to march, and Artabanus, who sleeps in the king's bed in the king's robes, sees the same dream and is convinced.

beats.scene: Thousands of men dig a long canal across a narrow neck of land
beats.summary: For four years Xerxes prepares his army, and his workers dig a canal through the neck of land at Mount Athos so that ships may avoid its storms.

beats.scene: Soldiers lash the water beside a broken bridge of ships
beats.summary: Xerxes has two bridges built across the Hellespont, and when a storm breaks them, he orders the sea to be whipped and chained, and builds new ones with ships.

beats.scene: A rich man in Sardis kneels before Xerxes, offering gold in a bowl
beats.summary: At Sardis the rich Lydian Pythius offers Xerxes all his wealth, and Xerxes, who is pleased, makes up the sum himself.

beats.scene: A king on a white marble throne watches a sea covered with ships
beats.summary: At Abydos Xerxes watches his army, and he weeps, since he reflects that none of his men will be alive in a hundred years.

beats.scene: Soldiers cross a long bridge of boats at sunrise as smoke rises
beats.summary: After a prayer to the sun, Xerxes pours wine into the sea, and his army takes seven days and nights to cross the bridges.

beats.scene: A king counts his troops in a huge circle of men on a plain
beats.summary: At Doriscus, Xerxes counts his army by packing ten thousand men into a fenced space, and Herodotus's total is far larger than modern scholars believe.

beats.scene: Ships crowd the sea as a queen steers her own vessel forward
beats.summary: Xerxes reviews his fleet of more than twelve hundred warships, and Herodotus praises Queen Artemisia of Halicarnassus, who sails with five ships.

beats.scene: Greek delegates stand together at a crossroads on a narrow strip of land
beats.summary: The Greek cities that will resist meet at the Isthmus and swear to fight together, but the rich ruler Gelon of Syracuse offers help only if he can command.

beats.scene: Athenians pour silver coins into a mould beside the sea
beats.summary: Themistocles persuades Athens to spend a rich find of silver on two hundred warships instead of sharing it out among the citizens.

beats.scene: A priestess at Delphi speaks in a dark temple to worried Athenians
beats.summary: The oracle at Delphi gives Athens two answers, the second telling the city to trust in a wooden wall, and Themistocles explains that it means ships.

beats.scene: Three Greek spies are led through a huge Persian camp by guards
beats.summary: Greek spies at Sardis are caught, but Xerxes orders them to be shown his whole army, and then sends them home.

beats.scene: Two Spartans bow their heads to the ground before a golden throne at Susa
beats.summary: Two Spartans, Sperthias and Bulis, go to Persia to pay for the heralds who were killed, and tell Xerxes that Greeks would never live as slaves.

beats.scene: Greek soldiers retreat from a high mountain pass as dust rises behind them
beats.summary: The Greeks go north to defend the Vale of Tempe, but when they learn that Persians can use another pass, they go home, and Thessaly joins Persia.

beats.scene: Lions attack baggage camels at night beside a river drying up
beats.summary: On the march through Macedonia, lions attack the baggage camels, the rivers run dry, and the cities that feed the army are ruined.

beats.scene: A fleet of Greek ships anchors off a rocky northern coast
beats.summary: The Greeks decide to hold the narrow pass at Thermopylae by land and the straits at Artemisium by sea, and Athens gives way to a Spartan admiral.

beats.scene: A Spartan king stands before three hundred chosen men
beats.summary: The oracle tells Sparta that either the city will fall or a king will die, and King Leonidas chooses three hundred men who have living sons.

beats.scene: Greek soldiers march along a coastal road toward a mountain pass
beats.summary: Leonidas marches north, and as he goes, soldiers from many cities join him until several thousand men hold the pass.

beats.scene: Greek officers argue in a camp beneath steep mountains and a wall
beats.summary: As the Persians draw near, the Peloponnesians want to retreat, but Leonidas decides to stay and sends for help.

beats.scene: A Persian rider watches Spartans combing their long hair by a wall
beats.summary: Xerxes sends a scout who finds the Spartans combing their hair, and Demaratus explains that it means they are ready to die.

beats.scene: Persian arrows fly in a cloud above a narrow pass at midday
beats.summary: A Spartan jokes that the Persian arrows are so many that they will hide the sun, and that it will be pleasant to fight in the shade.

beats.scene: Greek soldiers with shields stand shoulder to shoulder in a narrow pass
beats.summary: The Greeks hold the pass for two days, pretending to run and then turning on their pursuers, and Xerxes leaps from his throne in fear.

beats.scene: Persian soldiers climb a hidden mountain path through oak trees at night
beats.summary: A local man named Ephialtes shows Xerxes a path over the mountains, and the Immortals pass the Phocian guards at dawn.

beats.scene: A seer studies an animal sacrifice while Greek sentries run up from the hills
beats.summary: The seer Megistias reads the sacrifice and foretells death at dawn, and scouts arrive to say that the Persians are coming round.

beats.scene: Leonidas speaks to his men as other Greeks march away down the road
beats.summary: Leonidas sends most of the Greeks away, while the Thespians choose to stay and fight with him and the three hundred Spartans.

beats.scene: Greek soldiers charge down toward a crowd of Persians in a wider space
beats.summary: The Greeks move out to the wider ground, fight until their spears are broken, and Leonidas falls, but they drive the Persians back four times over his body.

beats.scene: Greek soldiers on a small hill defend themselves with their bare hands
beats.summary: The last Greeks retreat to a small hill and fight there with swords, hands and teeth, until the Persians finish them with arrows.

beats.scene: A sick Spartan soldier walks home alone past silent villagers
beats.summary: Aristodemus, a Spartan who was sent away with an eye illness, is shamed on his return, and he later wins back his honour.

beats.scene: Themistocles counts silver coins in a quiet corner of a ship's deck
beats.summary: At Artemisium the Euboeans pay Themistocles to keep the fleet there, and he shares a little of the silver with the commanders and keeps the rest.

beats.scene: Huge waves break on a rocky coast under black clouds
beats.summary: A great storm wrecks four hundred Persian ships, and the Athenians pray to the north wind, which they say is their son-in-law.

beats.scene: Greek ships and Persian ships crash together in a narrow channel
beats.summary: The Greeks fight three days at Artemisium, and then withdraw when they hear that Thermopylae has fallen, with Themistocles leaving messages on stones for the Ionians.

beats.scene: Persian officers listen to Arcadian soldiers beside a ruined pass
beats.summary: Arcadian deserters tell Xerxes that the Greeks are watching the Olympic games for a prize of an olive wreath, and a Persian asks what kind of men he is fighting.

beats.scene: Stones and lightning crash down on soldiers beneath a high cliff
beats.summary: As the Persians approach Delphi, lightning and falling rocks scatter them, and the Delphians say that two giant warriors chased them away.

beats.scene: Athenian families board small ships carrying bundles and children
beats.summary: The Athenians leave their city, sending their families to safe places, and the sacred snake of the Acropolis refuses its honey cake.

beats.scene: Persian soldiers climb a steep cliff behind the Acropolis in the dark
beats.summary: A few Athenians defend the Acropolis with barricades and rolling stones, but the Persians climb a hidden cliff and burn the temples.

beats.scene: A burned olive tree with a new green shoot among black ruins
beats.summary: Xerxes tells the Athenian exiles to make a sacrifice among the ruins, and they find the sacred olive tree has already sprouted a new shoot.

beats.scene: Greek commanders argue around a table while a ship sits at anchor
beats.summary: At Salamis the Greek commanders argue about whether to stay, and Themistocles tells the Corinthian Adeimantus that men who are last are never crowned.

beats.scene: A leader points at the horizon while others turn their faces away
beats.summary: Themistocles tells Eurybiades that the narrow waters of Salamis are the best place to fight, and that otherwise the Athenians will sail away to Italy, so the Spartan gives way.

beats.scene: A servant rows across the dark strait toward the Persian camp
beats.summary: Themistocles slips out of a quarrelsome council and sends his servant Sicinnus to tell Xerxes that the Greeks mean to flee, so that the Persians will block the straits.

beats.scene: A queen stands before a seated king in a tent at night
beats.summary: Xerxes asks his captains whether to fight at sea, and Artemisia alone advises against it, but Xerxes praises her and follows the majority.

beats.scene: A tall man in a plain cloak speaks with Themistocles beside a ship
beats.summary: The Athenian Aristides, who was exiled by the Athenians, crosses from Aegina to tell Themistocles that the Greeks are surrounded, and Themistocles says that it is his own doing.

beats.scene: Greek ships back away from a line of Persian ships at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn Themistocles speaks to the crews, and the Greek ships back water until an Athenian ship rushes forward and the fight begins.

beats.scene: A king sits on a hillside throne as scribes write down names
beats.summary: The huge Persian ships get in each other's way in the narrow strait, and Xerxes watches from a throne on the shore, while his scribes record who fights well.

beats.scene: A single ship rams another ship in the middle of a crowded strait
beats.summary: Queen Artemisia escapes an Athenian ship by ramming one of her own side's ships, and Xerxes, who is watching, thinks that she has sunk an enemy.

beats.scene: Greek sailors spear Persian soldiers on a small rocky island
beats.summary: The Greeks win the sea battle of Salamis, and Aristides lands on a small island and kills the Persian soldiers stationed there, while the Persians flee.

beats.scene: Soldiers weak with hunger march home through the mountains of Thrace
beats.summary: Xerxes, afraid that the Greeks will cut his bridges, goes home on Mardonius's advice and leaves him with a picked army, and the retreating soldiers starve.

beats.scene: Greek captains write names on stones while a man in an olive wreath watches
beats.summary: The Greek commanders vote for the bravest man of the war, and each votes for himself first, but nearly all vote for Themistocles second, and Sparta honours him with a crown.

beats.scene: A king's messenger speaks to Athenians in a city assembly
beats.summary: Mardonius sends Alexander of Macedon to offer Athens its land and independence, and the Athenians answer that they will never make peace as long as the sun follows its path.

beats.scene: Smoke rises over Athens as a Persian general studies the empty streets
beats.summary: In 479 BC Mardonius marches into Attica again, the Athenians leave their city a second time, and they warn Sparta that they will make peace unless help comes.

beats.scene: A tall man from Tegea speaks to Spartan leaders in a council chamber
beats.summary: The Spartans, busy with a festival and a wall across the Isthmus, delay, until Chileus of Tegea warns them that Athens may join Persia, and the army marches out that very night.

beats.scene: Greek soldiers from many cities march together beneath a high ridge
beats.summary: The Greek army gathers near Plataea, with about forty thousand heavy infantry from many cities, and the Athenians win the honour of holding the left wing.

beats.scene: Persian officers feast at a long table in the rich house of a Theban
beats.summary: At a dinner in Thebes, a Persian tells a Greek guest that few of his countrymen will live, and that the worst sorrow is to know and be powerless.

beats.scene: Persian horsemen charge, and one rider in gold armour falls from his horse
beats.summary: The Persian cavalry attacks, but its leader Masistius is killed, and the Persians mourn him by cutting their hair and their horses' manes.

beats.scene: A dry spring and a stranded supply train in a narrow mountain pass
beats.summary: For eleven days the armies wait, and the Persian horsemen cut the Greek supply route and spoil the Greek spring, so that the Greeks run short of food and water.

beats.scene: A Spartan officer drops a heavy stone at the feet of his general
beats.summary: During a night retreat, the Spartan Amompharetus refuses to run from foreigners and drops a stone at Pausanias's feet, and the army loses time.

beats.scene: Mardonius on a white horse points at the retreating Greeks with a sword
beats.summary: At dawn Mardonius sees the Greeks move, thinks they are running, taunts the Spartans for cowardice, and orders an attack.

beats.scene: Spartans kneel behind their shields as arrows fall on them in a field
beats.summary: The Spartans wait behind their shields as arrows fall, since the omens are bad, until at last the omens turn good and they charge.

beats.scene: Spartan and Persian soldiers fight hand to hand near a wooden fort
beats.summary: The Spartans charge, and Mardonius dies in the fight, struck by a stone, and the Persians run to their wooden fort, where the Athenians break in.

beats.scene: Two tables stand side by side in a Persian tent, one rich, one plain
beats.summary: Pausanias finds Xerxes's tent in the Persian camp, and has a rich Persian dinner and a plain Spartan dinner set side by side to show the Greeks how foolish the Persians were.

beats.scene: A bronze column in the shape of three twisting snakes holds a gold bowl
beats.summary: The Greeks divide the Persian treasure, give a tenth to the gods, and set up a golden tripod on a bronze column of snakes at Delphi.

beats.scene: Greek ships rest at anchor off a sunny island while a sailor speaks urgently
beats.summary: In 479 BC a man from Samos asks the Greek fleet to free the Ionians, and the fleet sails to Samos, where the Persians have beached their ships at Mycale.

beats.scene: Greek soldiers on a beach hear a herald's staff shining in the sand
beats.summary: As the Greeks march to the attack, a rumour spreads among them that Plataea has been won, and Herodotus says that the two battles were fought on the same day.

beats.scene: Greek soldiers storm a wooden stockade beside a line of burning ships
beats.summary: The Greeks win the battle of Mycale in 479 BC, the Ionians in the Persian army change sides, and the Persian ships are burned.

beats.scene: Greek delegates debate beside a harbour full of islanders' ships
beats.summary: The Greeks argue about moving the Ionians to Greece for safety, but the Athenians refuse, and the Samians, Chians and Lesbians join the alliance.

beats.scene: Starving Persian soldiers slip out of a besieged hilltop town at night
beats.summary: The Athenians besiege Sestos through the autumn, the starving Persians slip out, and the governor Artayctes is caught and put to death.

beats.scene: Athenian sailors carry great coils of rope across the sea in their ships
beats.summary: The Athenians sail home with the cables of the great bridge, which they set up as offerings in their temples.

beats.scene: An old man sets down his pen beside a scroll at dusk
beats.summary: Herodotus's story comes round to its start, with the lesson that no man's good fortune stays in one place, like a wheel that does not let the same men always prosper.

beats.scene: Cyrus and his Persian nobles stand on a rough stony hillside
beats.summary: Herodotus ends with Cyrus's warning that soft lands breed soft men.

A1A2: Herodotus of Halicarnassus wrote down old stories so that people would remember them.
People in Persia say that Phoenician sailors took a Greek princess named Io.
Then Paris of Troy took Helen, and the Greeks sailed to Troy to fight.
Herodotus does not know who began it, but he knows the first wrong.
Candaules, king of Lydia, was very proud of his beautiful wife.
The queen saw Gyges, and she told him to kill the king.
Croesus came from Gyges's family, and he fought the Greek cities.
Croesus wanted ships, but a wise man told him not to build them.
The Lydians were the first people to make coins of gold and silver.
A singer jumped into the sea, and a dolphin carried him home.
Solon of Athens made laws for his city and then left to travel.
Croesus showed Solon all his gold and asked him a big question.
Solon said, “Tellus of Athens,” and he told the king why.
Two brothers pulled their mother to the temple, then slept and never woke.
Solon said that no one is happy until he is dead.
Croesus sent Solon away, but then he had a terrible dream.
Croesus hid every spear and kept his son away from battles.
A wild boar was ruining farms, and Atys begged to go hunting.
In the hunt, Adrastus threw his spear and hit Atys by mistake.
Croesus was not angry with Adrastus, but Adrastus killed himself at the tomb.
King Astyages had a bad dream about his daughter, Mandane.
Then he dreamed of a vine that covered all the land.
A farmer and his wife saved the baby and hid him.
The boy was named Cyrus, and at ten he played at being king.
Cyrus punished a boy who would not obey, and the king noticed.
The farmer told the truth, and the king sent Cyrus to Persia.
Astyages was angry with Harpagus, and he punished him terribly.
Harpagus hid a letter in a dead hare and sent it to Cyrus.
Cyrus gave the Persians a hard day of work and then a feast.
The Medes fought the Persians, but many Medes joined Cyrus instead.
Croesus tested the oracles, and only Delphi gave the right answer.
Croesus sent huge gifts of gold to the temple at Delphi.
The oracle said that if he fought Persia, a great empire would fall.
Croesus asked which Greeks were strongest, and the answer was Sparta and Athens.
A wise man warned Croesus that the Persians were a hard people.
Croesus crossed the river Halys and fought a hard battle.
Croesus went home to Sardis and sent his soldiers away.
Cyrus put camels in front, and the Lydian horses were afraid.
The Persians surrounded Sardis, and one soldier found a way up the cliff.
Croesus's silent son spoke for the first time to save him.
Cyrus put Croesus on a pyre, but then a storm put out the fire.
Croesus sent a message to Delphi because the oracle had tricked him.
Cyrus told the Greeks a story about a man who played music for fish.
The people of Phocaea put their families on ships and left.
Persian boys learned to ride horses, to shoot arrows, and to tell the truth.
Cyrus went to fight Babylon, a city with huge walls and a river.
Cyrus turned the river aside and his soldiers walked into Babylon.
Cyrus attacked the Massagetae, a people led by Queen Tomyris.
Cyrus left food and wine in his camp, and the Massagetae drank it.
Queen Tomyris won the battle, and King Cyrus died.
Cambyses, son of Cyrus, wanted to take Egypt, the land of the Nile.
In Egypt, women went to market, and men stayed at home weaving.
The Egyptians loved their cats, and they cried when a cat died.
A king raised two babies in silence to see their first word.
Nobody could tell Herodotus where the great river Nile began.
A little bird cleans the teeth of a crocodile, Herodotus says.
Egyptian priests cleaned the body and wrapped it in white linen.
Thousands of men worked for years to build the great pyramid.
Two brothers found a secret way into the king's treasure room.
Herodotus saw a huge stone building with three thousand rooms.
Egyptian priests showed a Greek visitor three hundred and forty-five old statues.
The Egyptians were the first people to divide the year into twelve months.
Egyptian priests said that Helen never went to Troy at all.
Herodotus believed that Helen was in Egypt while the Greeks fought at Troy.
Amasis was not a noble, but the army made him king of Egypt.
Amasis made a statue from the gold bowl he washed his feet in.
Amasis worked in the morning, but in the evening he liked to laugh.
Thousands of Egyptians sailed down the river to a great festival.
Amasis gave the Greeks a town where they could trade with Egypt.
Herodotus told the story of the phoenix, a bird of fire.
A Greek soldier left Egypt and showed Cambyses how to cross the desert.
The Persians won the battle, and soon they took the city of Memphis.
The captured king did not cry, but he cried for an old friend.
The king of Ethiopia sent Cambyses a huge bow as his answer.
An army of fifty thousand men walked into the desert and was lost.
Cambyses laughed at Egyptian gods and hurt their sacred bull.
Cambyses had a bad dream about his brother Smerdis.
Polycrates ruled the island of Samos, and he had a strong fleet.
Polycrates threw his best ring into the sea, but it came back.
A Persian governor tricked Polycrates and brought about his end.
Cambyses heard that a false king had taken his throne, and then he died.
A Persian noble found out that the new king had no ears.
Seven Persian nobles promised to remove the false king.
The seven nobles went into the palace and killed the false king.
The nobles argued about the best way to rule the empire.
Seven horsemen waited, and the first horse to call would choose the king.
Darius became king, and a Greek doctor helped to heal his foot.
Darius divided his huge empire into twenty parts and fixed the taxes.
Riders carried the king's messages along a long road with many stations.
Darius asked Greeks and Indians about how they treated their dead.
The Scythians told a story about golden gifts that fell from the sky.
The Scythians had no cities, and they lived in wagons.
Darius crossed a bridge of boats over a wide river.
The Scythians sent Darius a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows.
The Scythians kept riding away, and Darius could not catch them.
A hare ran between the two armies, and the Scythians chased it.
Darius left in the night, and the Scythians rushed to the bridge.
Five young men crossed the desert and found a river with crocodiles.
Phoenician sailors sailed all the way around Africa, Herodotus was told.
Darius sent a captain to explore a great river in India.
Two friends killed the brother of the ruler of Athens.
The oracle told the Spartans to free the city of Athens.
Athens became a democracy, and the people ruled themselves.
A visitor showed the king of Sparta a map made of bronze.
The Athenians agreed to help the Ionians and sent twenty ships.
A secret message was written on the shaved head of a slave.
The Greek cities of Asia rose against the Persians in 499 BC.
The Greeks marched on Sardis and burned the city.
Darius ordered a servant to remind him about Athens each day.
The Persians beat the Greeks near Ephesus, and the Athenians sailed home.
A huge Persian fleet gathered to crush the Greek revolt.
The Ionians would not train, and many of their ships ran away.
Miletus fell to the Persians, and the Athenians wept over it.
After the revolt, the Persians treated the Ionian cities more fairly.
A great storm destroyed three hundred Persian ships near Mount Athos.
Athens and Sparta threw Persian messengers into a pit and a well.
Miltiades came home to Athens, and the people chose him as a general.
A Persian general burned incense on the altar of a holy island.
Eretria fought for six days, but two men opened the gates.
Hippias led the Persians to the plain of Marathon in Attica.
The runner Pheidippides asked Sparta for help, but the Spartans said wait.
The Athenian generals argued, and one man cast the deciding vote.
Soldiers from the small city of Plataea came to help the Athenians.
The Athenians ran across the plain, and the Persians thought they were mad.
Only a few Athenians died, but thousands of Persians lay dead.
Brave Athenians died, and one of them held a ship with his hand.
The Athenian army hurried back to Athens before the Persian ships.
The Spartans arrived too late, but they praised the Athenians.
Miltiades failed to take an island, and he was punished.
King Darius planned a bigger army, but he died before it was ready.
Xerxes did not want a war at first, but Mardonius did.
Xerxes told his nobles he would march on Greece, and one old man warned him.
A dream told Xerxes to march, and even Artabanus believed it.
Thousands of men dug a canal through the land beside a mountain.
Xerxes built bridges of boats, and when a storm broke them, he whipped the sea.
A very rich Lydian offered his gold to the king, and the king refused.
Xerxes saw his huge army and began to cry.
At sunrise Xerxes prayed, and his army crossed the sea on the bridges.
Xerxes counted his army at Doriscus, and the number was huge.
A fleet of twelve hundred ships passed before the king, and one captain was a woman.
Some Greek cities met and promised to stand together against Persia.
Themistocles told Athens to use its silver to build two hundred ships.
The oracle told the Athenians to trust a wall of wood.
Xerxes showed his huge army to some spies and sent them home.
Two Spartans went to Persia to say sorry for killing the heralds.
Greek soldiers went north to block a pass, but they came back.
Lions attacked the camels, and the army drank rivers dry.
The Greeks chose to defend a narrow pass and a narrow sea.
Sparta heard a terrible message, and King Leonidas chose three hundred men.
Soldiers from many cities joined Leonidas on the road north.
The Persians came near, and some Greeks wanted to go home.
A Persian scout saw the Spartans combing their long hair.
A Spartan said that the Persian arrows were so many they hid the sun.
The Greeks held the narrow pass for two days against Xerxes.
A traitor told the Persians about a secret path over the mountain.
A seer said that death would come at dawn, and scouts agreed.
Leonidas sent most of the Greeks home, but some chose to stay.
Leonidas and his men fought until the end, and the king fell.
The last Greeks fought on a hill until the Persians shot them.
One Spartan survived because he was sent home, but Sparta shamed him.
Themistocles took silver from the Euboeans and kept the Greek fleet there.
A great storm wrecked many Persian ships off a rocky coast.
The Greek ships fought for three days and then went away.
Deserters told the Persians that the Greeks were watching athletes at the Olympic Games.
A storm of rocks and lightning drove the Persians away from Delphi.
The Athenians left their city, and a sacred snake would not eat.
The Persians took the Acropolis of Athens and burned its temples.
A burned olive tree on the Acropolis grew a new green shoot.
The Greek leaders argued about whether to fight at Salamis or to retreat.
Themistocles said the Athenians would leave and found a new city.
Themistocles sent a secret message to the Persian king in the night.
Queen Artemisia told Xerxes not to fight a sea battle, but he did not listen.
An exile told Themistocles that the Greeks were surrounded by enemy ships.
At dawn the Greeks hesitated, and then one ship rowed forward and rammed.
Xerxes watched the battle from a throne on the shore.
Queen Artemisia escaped by ramming one of the king's own ships.
The Greeks won the battle, and the Persian ships ran away.
Xerxes went home, and many of his soldiers died of hunger.
The Greek commanders voted for the best man, and each chose himself.
The Athenians refused a Persian offer of peace.
In 479 BC Mardonius marched on Athens again, and the city was empty.
Sparta was slow to help, but then an army marched out at night.
A large Greek army gathered near the city of Plataea.
At a feast, a Persian said that many of them would soon die.
The Persian cavalry attacked, but their brave leader fell from his horse.
The Persian cavalry spoiled the Greeks' spring and cut off their food.
A Spartan refused to retreat, and he threw down a stone.
Mardonius saw the Greeks retreating and ordered his army to chase them.
The Spartans waited under a rain of arrows until the signs were good.
The Greeks won the battle, and Mardonius was killed.
Pausanias showed the Greeks a rich Persian dinner next to a poor Spartan dinner.
The Greeks gave a tenth of the treasure to the gods at Delphi.
A man from Samos asked the Greek fleet to free the Greeks of Ionia.
A rumour of the victory at Plataea reached the Greeks before their own fight.
The Greeks won at Mycale, and the Persian ships were burned.
The Greeks of Ionia joined the Greek alliance against Persia.
The Athenians took the city of Sestos, and the Persian governor was caught.
The Athenians took home the great cables of the bridge.
Herodotus believed that no king or country stays great for ever.
Cyrus said that soft land makes soft men, so the Persians stayed hard.
B1B2: Herodotus of Halicarnassus travels widely, asks questions of everyone he meets, and writes down what he is told. He wants the great deeds of Greeks and foreigners to be remembered, and he wants to explain why they went to war.

Persian storytellers say that Phoenician traders seized Io, the daughter of the king of Argos, and sailed away with her. The Greeks, they say, took the Phoenician princess Europa in return, and later Medea from the land of Colchis.

The Persians say that the Trojan prince Paris took Helen from Sparta, and that the Greeks then made war over a single woman. They add that Asia has felt hostile to the Greeks ever since the fall of Troy.

Herodotus cannot tell whether these old tales are true, so he begins with a man he knows did wrong to the Greeks. He promises to describe small cities as well as great ones, because good fortune never stays in one place.
The first man in the story is Croesus's ancestor, Candaules, king of Lydia. He is so proud of his wife's beauty that he orders his favourite guard, Gyges, to see her without her knowing it.

The queen noticed Gyges as he slipped away, and she understood who had planned the insult. Next day she gave him two choices, to die himself or to kill Candaules and take the throne, and Gyges chose to live.
Croesus becomes king of Lydia and attacks the Greek cities on the coast, beginning with Ephesus. In time he conquers them all, and from then on they must pay him tribute.
Croesus plans to build a fleet and attack the Greek islands. A wise Greek tells him that the islanders are buying horses to attack Sardis, and Croesus smiles and drops his plan.
Herodotus says the Lydians were the first people to use gold and silver coins and to keep shops. He also tells that in a long famine they played games on one day and ate on the next.

In the time of Croesus, the singer Arion sailed home to Corinth with a great deal of money. The sailors planned to kill him for it, but after one last song he leaped into the sea, and a dolphin carried him to land.
Solon, a wise Athenian, has given his city a new set of laws. He leaves on a long journey for ten years, so that nobody can ask him to change them, and in time he arrives at Sardis.
For three days the servants of Croesus show Solon the palace and its treasures. Then the king asks him who is the happiest man he has ever met, because he expects Solon to name him.
Solon answers that the happiest man was Tellus of Athens. Tellus lived in a rich city, saw all his children and grandchildren grow up, and died bravely in battle, so Athens buried him with honour.

Solon next names Cleobis and Biton of Argos, who pulled their mother's cart about eight kilometres to a festival of Hera. That night they fell asleep in the temple and never woke, and Argos set up statues of them at Delphi.
Croesus is angry that Solon places ordinary people above him. Solon replies that a long life is about 26,000 days and that no two are alike, so nobody is happy until the end.
Croesus thinks Solon a fool and sends him away. Soon afterwards he dreams that his son Atys, the better of his two sons, will be killed by an iron spear.

To protect Atys, Croesus finds him a wife, keeps him from war, and has every spear taken out of the men's rooms. At this time a stranger named Adrastus, an exiled prince from Phrygia, comes to the palace.

A huge boar is ruining the farms of Mysia, and Croesus sends hunters but keeps Atys at home because of his dream. Atys points out that a boar has no iron spear, so Croesus gives way and asks Adrastus to guard his son.
The hunters surround the boar, and Adrastus throws his spear at it. He misses, and the spear strikes Atys, so that the iron spear of the dream kills the king's son.

Croesus cries out to Zeus because his guest has killed his son, yet he forgives Adrastus, knowing that the gods planned it. Adrastus, who feels that he deserves to die, takes his own life at the tomb, and Croesus mourns for two years.

Astyages, king of the Medes, dreams that his daughter Mandane causes a flood that covers all of Asia. His wise men are alarmed, so he marries her to a quiet Persian named Cambyses, who seems too humble to be a danger.

A year later Astyages dreams that a vine grows from his daughter and covers the whole of Asia. When Mandane's son is born, the king calls his trusted officer Harpagus and orders him to take the baby and kill it.

Harpagus cannot bring himself to do it, and he orders the herdsman Mitradates to leave the child on the mountain. Mitradates's wife has just lost her own baby, so the two of them swap the infants and raise the prince as their son.
The boy grows up as Cyrus, the herdsman's son. At ten, he is chosen king in a game by the village boys, and he orders them about like a real ruler.
One of the boys, the son of a nobleman named Artembares, will not obey, and Cyrus has him whipped. The father complains to Astyages, who summons Cyrus and sees something familiar in the boy's face.

Astyages threatens the herdsman, who confesses, and the Magi tell the king that the dream has already come true in the boys' game. Astyages pretends to be relieved and sends Cyrus away to his real parents in Persia.
Astyages still wants revenge on Harpagus for disobeying him. He punishes his officer in a cruel way, by taking the life of his son, and Harpagus bows and says nothing.
Harpagus writes a letter to Cyrus and sews it into the body of a hare. A trusted servant dressed as a hunter carries it to Persia, where the letter urges Cyrus to lead the Persians against the king.
Cyrus orders the Persians to clear a thorny field in one day, and the next day he gives them a great feast. He asks them which day they liked better, and they all say the feast.
When Astyages leads his army against the rebels, Harpagus and many Medes desert to Cyrus. The Persians win the war about 550 BC, and Cyrus keeps the old king in his own house.
Croesus fears the rising power of Cyrus and decides to ask the gods for advice. First he tests the oracles, and he asks each of them what he is doing on the hundredth day.
Croesus is delighted, and he sends enormous gifts to Delphi. He sacrifices three thousand animals and sends gold bars, a gold lion and many bowls, so that the god will be kind to him.

Croesus asks whether he should attack Persia, and the priestess answers that if he crosses the river Halys he will destroy a great empire. He also hears that he should run when a mule becomes king of the Medes.

Croesus asks who are the strongest Greeks and is told about Sparta and Athens. Herodotus then tells how Peisistratus returned to Athens beside a tall woman dressed as the goddess Athena, and the people welcomed him.

A Lydian named Sandanis tells Croesus that the Persians wear leather trousers, drink only water and eat what they can find. He asks what Croesus can win from such poor people, but the king pays no attention.
Croesus marches east over the river Halys, and he attacks the city of Pteria. Cyrus brings his army, and the two sides fight a fierce battle that lasts all day and ends with no winner.
Croesus decides that his army is too small, and he retreats to Sardis. He sends his hired soldiers home for the winter and asks his allies to come in five months, but Cyrus follows him at once.

Croesus draws up his famous horsemen on the plain outside Sardis. Harpagus advises Cyrus to put the baggage camels in front, because horses cannot bear their smell, and the Lydian horses turn and run.

Cyrus surrounds Sardis for fourteen days and offers a reward to the first man to climb the walls. A soldier named Hyroeades sees a Lydian guard climb down the steep cliff to pick up a helmet, and he follows the same path.
As the Persians pour in, a soldier raises his spear at Croesus without knowing who he is. The king's son, who has been mute all his life, finds his voice and cries out, “Man, do not kill Croesus.”

Cyrus puts Croesus on a pyre, but the king cries out Solon's name three times, and Cyrus, curious, asks what it means. When Croesus explains, Cyrus orders the fire put out, and after Croesus prays to Apollo, a storm breaks and puts it out.
Croesus sends his chains to Delphi and asks why the god deceived him. The priestess says that nobody can escape fate, and that the mule was Cyrus, whose parents were a Mede and a Persian.

The Greeks of Ionia ask Cyrus for terms, but he answers with a fable about a piper who played music to fish. When the fish did not dance, he caught them in a net, and Cyrus means that the Ionians came too late.
Cyrus leaves Harpagus to conquer the Greek cities of Ionia. The people of Phocaea refuse to live under Persia and sail away, after swearing not to return until a lump of iron floats.

Herodotus says that Persian boys are taught three things: to ride, to shoot with a bow, and to tell the truth. The Persians build no temples, and they like to discuss important matters twice, once sober and once with wine.
Cyrus marches against Babylon, a huge city on the river Euphrates. Herodotus says its walls were wide enough for a four-horse chariot to turn on top, though his figures are probably too large.

Cyrus lets the Babylonians stay behind their walls, and he secretly digs a channel to turn the Euphrates into a marsh. The water falls, his soldiers wade along the river bed, and they enter Babylon in 539 BC during a festival.
Cyrus wants to defeat Queen Tomyris of the Massagetae, a people living east of the Caspian. She tells him to rule his own land, but Croesus advises Cyrus to cross the river and set a trap.

Cyrus dreams that young Darius has wings that shade Asia and Europe, so he sends Darius home to be watched. He leaves a camp full of food and wine, and the Massagetae, who do not know wine, drink until they fall asleep.

Tomyris sends a message to Cyrus telling him to give back her son, because she will give him his fill of blood. In the battle that follows, the Massagetae win, and Cyrus dies about 530 BC after a reign of twenty-nine years.

Cambyses, the son of Cyrus, prepares to invade Egypt, and Herodotus describes the land he is about to attack. He calls Egypt the gift of the Nile, because every summer the river floods the fields and leaves rich black mud behind.

Herodotus is amazed that in Egypt nearly everything is the opposite of what he knows. The women go to the market and trade, while the men stay at home and weave, and the Egyptians even write from right to left.

Herodotus says that the Egyptians treat some animals as sacred, and that cats are the most loved of all. If a house catches fire, people try to save the cats first, and when a cat dies naturally, the family shave their eyebrows in grief.

King Psammetichus wants to learn which people are the oldest in the world, so he tries an experiment. A shepherd raises two babies without ever speaking to them, and their first word sounds like the Phrygian word for bread.

Herodotus travels up the Nile as far as Elephantine, but nobody can tell him where the river begins. He rejects the Greek theories, such as melting snow, since he knows that Egypt and the lands to the south are hot.

Herodotus describes the crocodile and the hippopotamus, which the Greeks have never seen. He says a small bird hops into a crocodile's mouth and eats the creatures on its teeth, and the crocodile never harms it.

Herodotus describes three grades of embalming, from costly to cheap, with the body packed in natron salt for seventy days. At some rich feasts a small wooden mummy is shown to the guests, to remind them to enjoy life while they can.

Herodotus says that King Khufu built the great pyramid with the work of a hundred thousand men, who changed shifts every three months. Modern scholars have found that the builders were probably paid workers and not slaves.

In the story of King Rhampsinitus, a builder leaves a secret stone in the royal treasury for his sons to use. The brothers steal the king's silver, and when one is caught, the other must outwit the king.

Herodotus visits the Labyrinth, a huge building of three thousand rooms near Lake Moeris. He thinks it more wonderful than all the pyramids, but the guards will not let him enter the lower rooms, where the kings are buried.

A Greek writer named Hecataeus once boasted at Thebes that he could trace his family back sixteen generations to a god. The priests led him into a hall and showed him 345 wooden statues, each one a high priest who followed his father.
Herodotus says that the Egyptians were the first to divide the year into twelve months. They give each month thirty days and add five days at the end, and he thinks this is wiser than the Greek way.
The priests tell Herodotus a story about Helen that no Greek poet has told. A storm drove Paris and Helen to Egypt, they say, and King Proteus sent Paris away and kept Helen safe for her husband.
