The Trojans told the Greeks that Helen was not in Troy, but nobody believed them. Herodotus agrees with the Egyptian priests, because he thinks that the Trojans would have given Helen back rather than watch their sons die.

Amasis is a man of ordinary family who is sent to calm a rebellion against King Apries. A rebel puts a helmet on his head and hails him as king, and Amasis accepts, defeats Apries and takes the throne.
To win respect, Amasis has a golden footbath melted down and made into a statue of a god. When the Egyptians bow to it, he tells them it was once his footbath, and that his rank is just as new.

Amasis works hard in the morning, but in the afternoon he drinks with his friends and jokes. When people complain, he says that an archer who keeps his bow always bent will find it breaks, and men also need rest.

At Bubastis there is a joyful festival, and Herodotus says that 700,000 people go there by boat, men and women together. Some of the women play castanets and some of the men play flutes, and everyone sings and claps on the way.

King Amasis likes Greeks, and he lets them live at Naucratis, the one port in Egypt where they can trade. Herodotus believes that the names of many Greek gods came from Egypt, though scholars now think that is true of only a few.

The priests of Heliopolis tell of a bird called the phoenix, which comes only once in five hundred years. Herodotus has seen only a painting of it, and he says the story it carries is not quite believable.

Amasis dies, and his son Psammenitus becomes king just before the Persians arrive. A Greek officer named Phanes, who has quarrelled with the Egyptians, helps Cambyses by arranging for Arab chiefs to give water for the desert crossing.
The Persians defeat the Egyptians at Pelusium in 525 BC. Herodotus later visits the field and sees that Persian skulls are thin, while Egyptian ones are hard to crack with a stone.

Cambyses tests the defeated king Psammenitus, and he makes him watch his own daughter carry water as a servant. Psammenitus says nothing, but when he sees an old friend begging in the road, he weeps aloud.
Cambyses sends spies to Ethiopia with fine gifts, but the Ethiopian king knows they are spies. He hands them a huge bow and says that when the Persians can bend it easily, they may attack him.
Cambyses sends an army of 50,000 men to attack the oracle of Ammon in the desert. The Ammonians say that a great sandstorm buried them, and Herodotus reports that nobody ever saw them again.
Cambyses has little respect for Egyptian customs, and he stabs the sacred Apis bull in the leg with his dagger. The Egyptians are horrified, and Herodotus concludes that the king is mad.
Cambyses dreams that his brother Smerdis sits on the royal throne with his head touching the sky. He fears the dream, so he sends his trusted servant Prexaspes to Persia to kill Smerdis in secret.
Polycrates takes power in Samos with the help of his brothers, and soon rules alone. His hundred warships and his thousand archers make him so strong that he makes friends with King Amasis of Egypt.

Amasis warns Polycrates that he is too lucky, and he advises him to throw away his dearest possession. Polycrates throws a precious ring into the sea, but a fisherman soon brings him a large fish, and the ring is inside.

Amasis ends the friendship, since he is sure that so much luck will turn into disaster. Oroetes, a Persian governor, then invites Polycrates to the mainland with a promise of gold, and he is killed there.
In 522 BC a Magus who looks like Cambyses's dead brother Smerdis claims the throne of Persia. When Cambyses hears of it, he jumps on his horse, his sword wounds his leg, and the wound kills him.
The false Smerdis never leaves his palace and meets no one. Otanes, a great noble, suspects him, and he asks his daughter, who is one of the king's wives, to feel for his ears at night.

Otanes tells five other great nobles about the fraud, and they agree to act against him. Darius, who has just returned from Persia, joins them and insists that they must act that very day before anyone gives them away.

The seven nobles force their way into the palace and find the false king and his brother. After a short fight in a dark room, the Magus is killed, and angry Persians then attack the Magi across the city.

Five days after the death of the false king, the seven argue about the best form of government. Otanes speaks for rule by the people, Megabyzus for rule by a few, and Darius for rule by one good king.
The nobles agree that the one whose horse neighs first at sunrise will be king. Darius's clever groom, Oebares, brings the horse to the place the night before, and it neighs at dawn.

The other six nobles dismount and bow to Darius, who becomes king in 522 BC. Soon afterwards Darius twists his ankle badly, and Egyptian doctors fail to help, but a Greek slave named Democedes cures it.

Darius divides the huge empire into twenty provinces, each under a governor and each paying a fixed tax. India, the farthest east, pays in gold dust, and the Persians call Darius the shopkeeper because he counts everything.

The Royal Road runs from Sardis to the Persian city of Susa, and it has stations all along the way. At each one, a fresh rider and a fresh horse take the message on, so that nothing travels faster over land.

Darius asks some Greeks if they would eat their dead fathers for a reward, and they say never. Some Indians, asked if they would burn their dead, are just as shocked, so Herodotus concludes that custom is king.
Darius decides to punish the Scythians, a people who once invaded Asia. Herodotus tells their story of the first king, in whose time a gold plough, yoke, axe and cup fell from the sky.
Herodotus explains that the Scythians have no towns and no farms, and that they live in wagons and ride horses. Their homes can move at any moment, and so no enemy can easily catch them.

Darius takes his army over the Bosporus on a bridge built by Mandrocles of Samos, and he marches to the Danube. The Ionian Greeks build a bridge of boats, and Darius orders them to guard it for sixty days.
The Scythians send Darius a strange gift of a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows. Darius thinks it means they are giving in, but his adviser Gobryas says it is a warning.

The Scythians draw the Persian army across their wide plains, driving off their cattle and filling the wells. Their king Idanthyrsus sends Darius a proud answer, telling him that they have no cities to lose and will fight when they please.
At last the two armies stand in lines facing each other, but a hare runs across the field. The Scythians chase it with shouts, and Darius realises that they do not respect him at all.

Darius leaves his camp at night, with fires burning and donkeys braying to deceive the enemy. The Scythians rush to the bridge and ask the Ionians to leave, but the Greek tyrants, led by Histiaeus, decide to stay loyal to Darius.
Herodotus describes Libya and the people who live there. Five young Nasamonians cross the great desert and find a river with crocodiles, which some think was the Niger.

King Necho of Egypt sends Phoenician sailors down the Red Sea, and in the third year they come back through the Pillars of Heracles. Herodotus does not believe that the sun was on their right, though that is exactly what would happen.
Darius sends a Greek captain named Scylax down the great river Indus to see where it goes. Scylax sails to the sea and then west to Egypt, and Darius conquers the Indian lands.

Athens is ruled by Hippias and his brother Hipparchus, the sons of Peisistratus. In 514 BC two friends, Harmodius and Aristogeiton, kill Hipparchus, but Hippias stays in power and rules more harshly than before.

A noble family of Athens, the Alcmaeonids, build a fine new front for the temple at Delphi. Every time the Spartans consult the oracle, the priestess tells them to free Athens, and in 510 BC they drive Hippias out.

A noble named Cleisthenes wins the people's favour and gives Athens a new government. He divides the citizens into ten tribes, and every man gets a share in ruling, so that the city becomes a democracy.

Aristagoras of Miletus visits Sparta and shows King Cleomenes a bronze map of the world, asking for help against Persia. When Cleomenes learns that Susa is three months' journey from the sea, he tells the visitor to leave.

Aristagoras speaks to a crowd of thirty thousand Athenians, and Herodotus remarks that it is easier to fool many than one. Athens votes to send twenty ships, which Herodotus calls the beginning of evils for Greeks and foreigners.
Histiaeus is stuck at the court of Darius, but he wants the Ionians to rise. He shaves a trusted slave's head, writes the order to revolt on it, and sends him to Miletus once the hair has grown back.

Aristagoras decides to give up his own power and announces that Miletus will be a democracy. The other Ionian cities throw out the tyrants who rule them for Persia, and the whole coast joins the revolt.
In 498 BC the Greek force marches to Sardis and takes the lower city. A soldier sets fire to a house with a reed roof, the flames spread, and the temple of the goddess Cybele is burned too.
When Darius hears about the burning of Sardis, he asks who the Athenians are. He shoots an arrow into the sky and orders a servant to say “Master, remember the Athenians” at every dinner.
The Persians catch up with the Greeks near Ephesus and defeat them. The Athenians then take their ships home and refuse to help again, although the revolt spreads to Cyprus and other places.

By 494 BC the Persians have gathered a huge army and a fleet of Phoenician ships to crush Miletus. The Ionian Greeks meet at Lade, a little island near the city, with three hundred and fifty-three ships.

A captain from Phocaea named Dionysius trains the Ionian fleet hard for a week. The Ionians complain about the work and refuse to go on, and during the battle of Lade the Samians sail away, so the Persians win.
The Persians take Miletus, and many of its people are carried away to Persia. When the Athenian writer Phrynichus puts the fall of Miletus on the stage, the audience weeps, and he is fined.

After the revolt, Persia learns some lessons and rules Ionia more fairly. The governor Artaphernes makes the Ionian cities settle their quarrels in court, measures their land and fixes taxes at much the same level as before.

In 492 BC Mardonius leads a Persian army and fleet along the coast toward Greece. A great storm wrecks the fleet off Mount Athos, with a loss of about three hundred ships and twenty thousand men, and Mardonius turns back.
In 491 BC Darius sends heralds to ask the Greek cities for earth and water as a sign of surrender. Many cities agree, but Athens throws the heralds into a pit and Sparta throws them into a well.

Miltiades is an Athenian who ruled the Chersonese for years under the Persians, and he escaped from the Persian fleet in 493 BC. In Athens he is accused of tyranny, but he is freed and elected a general.

In 490 BC a Persian fleet sails under Datis and Artaphernes, crossing the sea island by island. At Delos, Datis refuses to harm the holy island, and burns a great quantity of frankincense on the altar.

The Persians land on the island of Euboea and attack the city of Eretria. The Eretrians fight bravely for six days, but two traitors open the gates, and the Persians burn the temples and carry the people to Persia.

Hippias leads the Persians to Marathon, a plain by the sea in Attica where horses can move easily. As the soldiers land, he sneezes so hard that a tooth falls into the sand, and he takes it as a bad sign.

The Athenians send a runner named Pheidippides to ask Sparta for help, and he covers about two hundred and forty kilometres in two days. On the way he meets the god Pan, but the Spartans say they cannot march until the moon is full.
The ten Athenian generals cannot agree whether to fight or to wait for Sparta. Miltiades goes to Callimachus, the war leader, who has the deciding vote, and he persuades him to vote for battle.
Soldiers from the little city of Plataea arrive to help the Athenians. The generals give up their days of command to Miltiades, but he waits for his own day before he attacks.

In the narrow strait, the big Persian fleet cannot move, and its ships crash into each other. Xerxes watches from a throne under Mount Aigaleos, and his scribes write down the names of the captains who fight well.

By evening the Persian fleet is in full retreat, and the Greek ships hunt the survivors. Aristides lands soldiers on the little island of Psyttaleia, where Xerxes had placed Persian troops, and he kills them all.

The Persian cavalry attacks the Greeks, and their leader Masistius, who wears gold armour, falls from his wounded horse and is killed. The Persians mourn him by cutting off their own hair and the manes of their horses.

For eleven days the armies face each other, and neither will begin the fight because the omens are bad. The Persian horsemen cut off a Greek supply train and spoil the spring, and the Greeks are soon short of food and water.

At dawn Mardonius sees the Greeks withdrawing, and he supposes they are running away. He taunts the Spartans for being cowards after their fine words, and he orders his whole army to chase them.

The Spartans crouch behind their shields as the Persians fire arrow after arrow at them. Pausanias will not let them move until the sacrifices are good, so he prays to Hera, and at last the signs turn favourable.

The Spartans charge, and the Persians fight bravely but they have no armour and cannot match the Greek skill. Mardonius is killed, and the Persians run to their wooden fort, where the Greeks follow and take it.
After the battle, Pausanias finds the rich tent of Mardonius, full of gold and silver. He has a Persian dinner set beside a plain Spartan meal and laughs that the Persians came to rob such poor men.
The Greeks divide the Persian treasure and give a tenth to the gods. At Delphi they set up a golden tripod on a bronze column of three twisting snakes, and part of it still stands in Istanbul.
The Greek fleet, under the Spartan king Leotychides, lies at Delos. A man from Samos says that the Ionians will rise if the Greeks come, so the fleet sails to meet the Persians.
As the Greeks march along the shore, a rumour runs through the ranks that Mardonius has been beaten. Herodotus says that the news was true, and that the two battles were fought on the same day.
The Athenians and others attack first, and the Ionian Greeks in the Persian army change sides. The Persians run to their stockade, the Greeks break in, and then they burn the Persian ships.

After Mycale, the Peloponnesians say the Ionians should leave Asia and move to Greece. The Athenians refuse to give up their own people, and the Samians, Chians and Lesbians swear an oath to join the alliance.

The Greek fleet finds the bridges already broken, so the Spartans go home, but the Athenians besiege Sestos, where the governor Artayctes hides. At last the starving Persians slip away, and Artayctes is caught and put to death.

The Athenians pack up the great cables of the bridge across the Hellespont, and they sail home with them. They keep them as treasures, and some of them will hang in the temples, to remind their children of the war.
Looking back over the story, Herodotus sees that fortune never stays in one place, as Solon warned Croesus. Croesus later tells Cyrus the same thing, that human affairs turn like a wheel.
Herodotus ends his book with a story about Cyrus. When some Persians suggest moving to a softer, richer land, Cyrus replies that soft lands breed soft men, so they stay in their rough country.
C1C2: Some twenty-five centuries ago, a Greek named Herodotus, born in the coastal city of Halicarnassus, set out to gather the stories of the known world. He called his work an inquiry, for he questioned travellers, priests and soldiers, and weighed carefully what each of them told him. His purpose, as he declared at the outset, was that the great deeds of Greeks and foreigners alike should not fade from memory, and that people should understand why the two sides came to blows.

The learned men of Persia, Herodotus reports, say that the quarrel began when Phoenician traders landed at Argos and carried off the king's daughter Io. Some time afterwards, they add, certain Greeks sailed to Phoenicia and took the princess Europa, and then went on to Colchis and took Medea, who was the daughter of its king. Herodotus notes that the Phoenicians tell the story of Io differently, and he repeats both versions without taking a side.

In the Persian account, Paris, a prince of Troy, carried off Helen from her husband's house in Sparta, and the Greeks answered by raising a great army and crossing the sea to destroy his city. The Persians thought it foolish to go to war for the sake of one woman, since sensible men do not trouble themselves over women who are stolen. Yet they date their own enmity toward the Greeks from the fall of Troy, because they claim Asia and its peoples as their own.

Herodotus declines to say which of the old stories is true, for he prefers to begin with the first man whom he himself knows to have wronged the Greeks. From that point he will go on through the affairs of cities both great and small, since those that were mighty long ago have mostly become small, and those that are mighty in his own day were once weak. He is convinced that human prosperity never stays in the same place, and that is the thread running through the whole of his work.

The story starts with Candaules, an ancestor of Croesus and king of Lydia, who was so besotted with his wife's beauty that he could not stop boasting of it. Believing that no one would trust his words without proof, he commanded his favourite bodyguard, Gyges, to hide in the royal bedroom and see her for himself. Gyges protested that it was shameful, but the king would not hear a refusal.

The queen caught sight of Gyges as he crept away, and she guessed at once that her husband had arranged the dishonour. She summoned Gyges the next day and gave him a stark choice, either to die for what he had seen or to kill the king and take both his throne and his wife. Gyges, after pleading in vain, chose to live, and the Oracle at Delphi later approved his rule while warning that vengeance would fall on his fifth descendant, who proved to be Croesus.

When Croesus inherited the throne, he set about attacking the Greek cities of the coast one by one, beginning with Ephesus, and finding a pretext against each. He conquered them all in time, both the Ionians and the Aeolians, and compelled them to pay tribute. He was the first foreigner, as far as Herodotus knows, to take Greek subjects in this way, and until then the Greeks of Asia had been free.

Having mastered the mainland, Croesus gave orders for a fleet to be built so that he could attack the Greek islands. A wise Greek, either Bias of Priene or Pittacus of Mytilene, told him that the islanders were buying ten thousand horses to ride against Sardis. Croesus, who assumed that they would be foolish to try it, was amused by the idea, and the islanders were glad to become his friends instead.

Herodotus tells us that the Lydians were the first people to strike coins of gold and silver, and the first to keep shops, which perhaps explains the fabulous wealth of their kings. They also claimed to have invented dice, knucklebones and ball games during a famine so long that they played on one day to forget their hunger and ate only on the next. This lasted, so the story goes, for eighteen years, and it is only a story, though a charming one.

From these years Herodotus tells a story of Arion, a famous singer of Lesbos who earned a fortune in Italy and Sicily and then hired a Corinthian ship to carry him home. The sailors decided to throw him overboard and keep the money, and Arion, who was allowed one last song, sang it in his full costume and then leaped into the waves. A dolphin, charmed by the music, bore him to land, and he reached Corinth before the ship, where the sailors were forced to confess to the king.

To make sure that nobody could ask him to change them, he sailed away to see the world, and his travels took him to Egypt and then to Sardis. Croesus, who was then at the height of his power, welcomed the stranger into his palace as a guest.

On the third or fourth day, the servants of Croesus led Solon through the treasuries, showing him every great and beautiful thing that the king possessed.
