The trick worked completely, for the Lydian horses wheeled in terror, and the Lydians dismounted and fought on foot until they were driven back into the city.

For fourteen days the siege continued, until Cyrus promised a prize to the first man to scale the walls, and for a time nobody could find a way. Then a soldier named Hyroeades saw a Lydian guard climb down a steep cliff to pick up a fallen helmet, a part of the wall which the Lydians had left unguarded because they thought nobody could climb it. He climbed the same path, others followed, and the citadel of Sardis fell about 546 BC.

As the Persians flooded through the streets, a soldier ran toward Croesus with his spear raised, not knowing who he was, and the king, worn out by grief, did not even try to avoid the blow. His son, who had never spoken a word in his life, was so terrified that he found his voice and cried out to the man not to kill Croesus. It was the first sentence that he ever uttered, and he is said to have kept the power of speech for the rest of his life.

Cyrus had Croesus bound and set on a great pile of wood, and as the flames rose, the king groaned and cried out the name of Solon three times. Cyrus asked through his interpreters whom he meant, and on hearing of the Athenian's warning he reflected that he too was a man burning one who had been as fortunate as himself. The fire had taken hold, however, and only when Croesus called on Apollo did a storm burst from a clear sky and quench it, so Cyrus kept him as a trusted adviser.

Croesus sent his chains to Delphi and asked, with some bitterness, whether the Greek gods were always ungrateful. The priestess answered that not even a god can escape what is fated, that Apollo had delayed the fall of Sardis for three years, and that Croesus had never asked which empire he would destroy. As for the mule, she said, it was Cyrus, whose mother was a Mede of royal blood and whose father was a Persian, and Croesus admitted that the fault was his own.

The Ionian Greeks, who had refused to rebel against Croesus when Cyrus asked, now begged to be treated as they had been under the Lydians. Cyrus answered with a fable of a piper who played on the shore and called on the fish to come out and dance, and who, when they would not, took a net and hauled them in. When a Spartan herald forbade him to harm any Greek city, Cyrus scoffed that he did not fear men who kept a market in the middle of their towns to cheat one another.

While Cyrus turned to other conquests, Harpagus attacked the Greek cities of Ionia one by one, building ramps against their walls and taking them with ease. The people of Phocaea, who would not live as the subjects of a Persian master, put their families, their goods and the statues of their gods on their ships and sailed away to the west. Before they left, they sank a lump of iron in the sea and swore that they would not return to Phocaea until it floated, though more than half of them were homesick and returned all the same.

Herodotus, who admired many of the customs he found abroad, describes the Persians as a people who built no temples and who held that the whole sky was the dwelling of their god. Boys were taught three things between the ages of five and twenty: to ride, to shoot the bow, and to speak the truth. Important decisions were debated twice, first at table with wine and again in the sober light of morning, and a plan was kept only if it seemed good both times.

On the road to Babylon, one of the sacred white horses of Cyrus drowned in the river Gyndes, and the furious king spent a whole summer cutting the river into three hundred and sixty channels. At Babylon, Herodotus says, he found a square city with the Euphrates flowing through its middle and walls wide enough for a four-horse chariot to turn about on top. Modern scholars think his figures too large, but no one doubts that it was the greatest city of the age.

The Babylonians laughed at the besiegers from behind their walls, until Cyrus dug a channel and drained the Euphrates into a marsh, so that the river sank to a man's thigh. His soldiers waded in beneath the walls, and Herodotus says that the Babylonians were dancing and feasting at a festival, so that the outskirts of the city had fallen before the people in the centre knew of it. It was in this way, in 539 BC, that Babylon was taken for the first time.

Cyrus next turned against the Massagetae, a people of the eastern plains ruled by a widowed queen named Tomyris, and he began by building bridges across the river Araxes. Tomyris sent a herald warning him to leave her alone and rule his own people in peace, and offering to withdraw three days' march so that the armies might meet on her side of the river. Croesus, who was still among his advisers, urged Cyrus to accept, and to prepare a trap.

Once across the river, Cyrus dreamed that Darius, the young son of Hystaspes, had wings on his shoulders that shaded Asia and Europe, and he sent Hystaspes home to keep watch on his son. Then, following the advice of Croesus, he left the weakest of his men in a camp laid out with a rich feast and plenty of wine and withdrew. The Massagetae, who had never tasted wine, drank until they were helpless, and the Persians returned and killed many of them, among them the queen's son Spargapises.

Tomyris, grieving for her son, sent word to Cyrus that if he did not leave she would give him his fill of blood, since he was so hungry for it. The battle that followed was, in Herodotus's opinion, the fiercest ever fought between foreigners, with the two sides shooting arrows until they ran out and then fighting with spears and daggers. The Massagetae won, and Cyrus fell after a reign of twenty-nine years, about 530 BC, though Herodotus admits that other writers tell of his death differently.

Cyrus was succeeded by his son Cambyses, who resolved to conquer Egypt, and Herodotus pauses to describe the strange and ancient land that lay before the Persians. He called Egypt the gift of the river, since every summer the Nile rose and spread over the valley and the delta, and when it withdrew, it left behind a layer of rich dark mud. Farmers there, he noticed, hardly needed to plough, for they simply scattered the seed on the soft ground and waited for the harvest.

Herodotus, who had grown up among Greeks, was struck by how many Egyptian customs seemed the reverse of his own. The women went out to the market and ran the shops, he reports, while the men stayed at home and sat at the loom, and the men carried loads upon their heads while the women carried them on their shoulders. They wrote from right to left instead of left to right, and they ate in the street but did their private business at home, which amused him greatly.

The Egyptians, Herodotus reports, held many animals sacred, among them cats, dogs, ibises and crocodiles, and whoever killed one on purpose could be put to death. When a house caught fire, the people stood in a ring to save the cats before they tried to save the house, and if a cat died in the course of nature, the family shaved their eyebrows in mourning. The dead cats were carried to holy places, embalmed, and buried in the town of Bubastis.

The priests of Memphis told Herodotus that King Psammetichus once wished to learn which nation was the oldest, so he gave two newborn babies to a shepherd and ordered that nobody should ever speak a word in their hearing. After two years the children held out their hands to the shepherd and cried “becos”, which the king discovered was the Phrygian word for bread, and the Egyptians concluded that the Phrygians were an older people than themselves. Herodotus, as usual, claims no more than to report what he was told, and he adds that the Greeks told the story rather differently.

Herodotus asked every Egyptian, Libyan and Greek he met where the Nile began, but nobody could tell him, and he went up the river himself as far as Elephantine, the southern edge of Egypt. He listened to what Greek thinkers had said about the yearly flood, and rejected the idea that it came from melting snow, for in such hot lands he could not believe that snow would be found. The true cause, heavy summer rain in the highlands far to the south, was not understood by the Greeks of his time.

The crocodile, Herodotus says, spends its days on the land and its nights in the water, and some Egyptians treat it as a god while others hunt it as an enemy. He reports, though he did not see it himself, that a small bird goes into the crocodile's open mouth to feed on the leeches there, and that the crocodile, pleased by the cleaning, never harms it. Of the hippopotamus, he adds, the Greeks had no knowledge, and so he described it as a river horse.

Herodotus explains that Egyptians preserved their dead in three ways, the most expensive of which was reserved for people of rank. The body was cleaned, packed in natron salt for seventy days, and then wrapped from head to foot in strips of fine linen and returned to the family, who sealed it in a wooden case shaped like a man. At rich men's feasts, he adds, a servant carried round a small carved mummy and told the guests to drink and be merry, since this was what they would become.

Khufu, the king who built the great pyramid, was remembered by the Egyptians as a hard ruler, and Herodotus reports that he closed the temples and forced the people to work for him. Herodotus says that a hundred thousand men laboured in turn, each gang working for three months, and that it took ten years to build the road for the stones and twenty to raise the pyramid itself. Modern archaeologists have found the workers' villages and have shown that the builders were probably fed and paid labourers rather than slaves.

Herodotus repeats a tale about King Rhampsinitus, whose treasury was built by a mason who left a movable stone in the wall and told his two sons the secret as he lay dying. The brothers stole the king's silver again and again, until one of them was caught in a trap, and begged the other to leave him and keep the family safe. The surviving thief then outwitted the guards, stole the body, and so impressed the king that he offered him his daughter in marriage.

Beside Lake Moeris, Herodotus visited a building which the Greeks called the Labyrinth, and which twelve kings had built together, and he declared that it was a greater wonder than the pyramids. It had three thousand rooms, half of them above the ground and half beneath it, and he was allowed to walk through the upper rooms, which seemed to him a marvel of passages and courts. The guards would not allow him to enter the lower rooms, where the kings who built it were buried, and so he was obliged to rely on report.

At Thebes, Herodotus was told, the Greek writer Hecataeus once proudly recited his family tree, which went back sixteen generations to a god. The priests of Egypt were not impressed, and they led him into a great hall and showed him three hundred and forty-five wooden statues, each of a high priest who had been the son of the one before. None of them, they said, had been a god, and the lesson was that Egypt had a far longer past than any Greek could claim.

Herodotus believed that the Egyptians were the first people to reckon the year, and that they divided it into twelve months of thirty days each, adding five extra days at the end so that the seasons came round on time. The Greeks, he points out, add a whole month every second year to keep their calendar in step, and he thought the Egyptian method the more sensible of the two. It is one more sign of how closely the Egyptians watched the sky and how carefully they kept their records of the seasons.

The priests of Memphis gave Herodotus a version of the story of Helen that no Greek poet had told. After stealing Helen, they said, Paris had been blown off course by storms and had landed on the coast of Egypt, where the servants reported his crime to King Proteus. Proteus declared that he would have put the prince to death if he had not been a guest, and he ordered him to leave within three days while he kept Helen and her treasure safe for her husband.

When the Greeks arrived at Troy, the Trojans told them that Helen was not inside the walls, but nobody believed them, and the war continued until the city was destroyed. Herodotus agrees with the priests, for he cannot imagine that Priam and his sons would have risked their lives and their city for the sake of a woman who was not even there. He believes that the gods let the war run its course so that men might see that great wrongs are followed by great punishments.

Amasis was a common soldier, and when King Apries sent him to calm a rebellion, one of the rebels placed a helmet on his head as a sign of kingship. Amasis accepted the honour at once, gathered the rebels around him, and defeated Apries in battle. Many Egyptians, who knew that he had come from a humble family, did not at first respect him.

To win the respect of his subjects, Amasis took the golden basin in which he and his guests washed their feet, and had it melted down and made into a statue of a god. The Egyptians bowed down before the statue with great reverence, and Amasis then told them that it had once been a footbath, and that he himself had been an ordinary man before he became king. The lesson was understood at once, and from that day the people honoured their new king as they had never honoured him before.

Amasis, Herodotus tells us, did the business of the kingdom in the morning, and in the afternoon he drank with his friends and made jokes. His advisers thought this unbecoming in a king, but Amasis replied that archers keep their bows strung only when they are using them, because a bow that was always bent would snap when the need came. He said that the same was true of men, and that anyone who never played would end by going mad.

Herodotus describes the festival of Bubastis as the most cheerful of all those held in Egypt, since the people travelled to it in crowded boats, men and women together, with music and laughter all the way. Some of the women played castanets while some of the men played pipes, and as they passed each town on the river, the women called out jokes to the people on the bank. At the temple, Herodotus says, more wine was drunk in a single day than in the rest of the year, and he put the number of visitors at seven hundred thousand.

Amasis was friendly to the Greeks, and he gave them the town of Naucratis on the Nile, which he made the only port where merchants from the Greek world could land and trade. Herodotus, who was impressed by the antiquity of Egypt, declared that the names of most of the Greek gods had come from there, a claim which later scholars have judged true of only a few of them. Yet the trading town was a meeting place of two worlds, and many Greeks learned about Egypt through it.

At Heliopolis the priests told Herodotus of a sacred bird called the phoenix, which comes only once in five hundred years, carrying the body of its dead father in an egg of myrrh to the temple of the sun. Herodotus admitted that he had seen it only in a painting, and that he did not find the story believable. Yet he ended his account of Egypt by declaring that it possessed more wonders than any other land, and works too great for words to describe.

Amasis died just before the Persians arrived, and the throne passed to his son Psammenitus, who ruled for only six months. Cambyses, who had to cross a waterless desert to reach Egypt, was helped by Phanes, a Greek officer who had quarrelled with the Egyptians and defected. At his suggestion the king asked the Arabs, who controlled the road, for safe passage, and they ensured that his army had water by sending it across the sand in skins carried on camels.

At Pelusium, in 525 BC, the Persians defeated the Egyptians after a hard fight and then advanced on Memphis, which fell soon afterwards. Years later, Herodotus walked over the battlefield, where the bones of the two sides still lay apart, and found Persian skulls so thin that a pebble would break them. Egyptian skulls, by contrast, were so hard that a stone could hardly crack them, and the local people explained that Egyptians shaved their heads from childhood, while the Persians always wore soft caps.

To test his prisoner, Cambyses made Psammenitus sit beside the road and watch his daughter pass in a servant's dress and his son led away to execution, yet the Egyptian king did not weep. But when an old friend, now poor, passed by and begged for alms, Psammenitus wept and struck his head, and Cambyses asked him why. The old king answered that his own troubles were too great for tears, while the sorrow of a friend fallen from wealth was something he could cry over.

Cambyses now planned to conquer the Ethiopians, and sent spies to their country with gifts of a purple robe, a gold necklace and a jar of palm wine. The Ethiopian king, who saw at once that they were spies, laughed at the presents and gave the messengers a huge bow, telling them that when the Persians could bend such a bow with ease, they might attack him. Cambyses marched without enough food and was forced to turn back when his army ran out of supplies.

Cambyses also sent an army of fifty thousand men across the desert to destroy the oracle of Ammon at the oasis now called Siwa, and the soldiers set out from Thebes and were never seen again. The Ammonians told Herodotus that a strong south wind had risen as the army ate its midday meal and buried every man under the sand. Herodotus reports the story as it was told to him, and no trace of that army has ever been found.

The Egyptians were celebrating the appearance of a new Apis bull, a sacred animal believed to be a god, when Cambyses returned from a failed expedition and took their joy for mockery of his misfortune. He drew his dagger and stabbed the bull in the thigh, and it died of the wound and was buried in secret by the priests. Herodotus concluded that the king was mad, and he added that only a madman could laugh at the sacred laws and customs of other peoples.

At about this time Cambyses dreamed that a messenger came from Persia to tell him that his brother Smerdis sat upon the royal throne, with his head touching the sky. Fearing that the brother would take his place, he sent a trusted officer named Prexaspes to Persia to put Smerdis to death in secret. When Croesus warned him to restrain his violent temper, the king was so enraged that he seized a bow and tried to shoot the old man, who fled from the room.

Polycrates, who seized the island of Samos with the help of two brothers and then took sole power, built up a fleet of a hundred ships and a force of a thousand archers. He raided friend and foe alike, saying that he gained more by returning plunder than by never taking it, and he became so strong that the pharaoh Amasis sought his friendship. Herodotus says that the Samians built three of the greatest works in the Greek world: a tunnel through a mountain, a sea wall in the harbour and the biggest temple he had ever seen.

Amasis, who feared that such steady good fortune would draw the jealousy of the gods, advised Polycrates to throw away the thing he treasured most. Polycrates took his favourite emerald ring and flung it from a boat into the sea, but days later a fisherman brought him a splendid fish, and the cooks found the ring inside it. Polycrates wrote to Amasis with delight, and the pharaoh, convinced that he was doomed, ended their friendship.

Amasis broke off the friendship, saying that he did not wish to grieve for a friend whose fall he could foresee, and the Samian's luck soon began to fail. Oroetes, a Persian governor who hated him, sent word that Cambyses was plotting against him and that he would share his gold with Polycrates in return for refuge, and Polycrates, who loved treasure, sailed to the mainland against all advice. There he was killed and his body displayed, and Herodotus says that his end was unworthy of his great ambitions.

While Cambyses was still in Syria, a Magus who bore a striking resemblance to the dead Smerdis seized the throne in Persia and claimed to be the king's brother. When the news reached Cambyses, he leaped upon his horse in a rage, and the sword at his side slipped from its sheath and wounded his thigh in the very place where he had stabbed the Apis bull. The wound turned bad, and he died soon afterwards at a town called Ecbatana, a name that an oracle had once warned him about, and which he had wrongly believed to be the Median city of that name.

The false Smerdis was clever, for he cancelled taxes and military service for three years, which made him popular, but he never left the palace and received almost nobody. A noble named Otanes grew suspicious, and he asked his daughter Phaedymia, who belonged to the king's household, to feel for the king's ears while he slept. Cyrus had once cut off the ears of a Magus for some crime, and Phaedymia found that the king had none, so Otanes knew that the man on the throne was an impostor.

Otanes shared his secret with five other great Persian nobles, Aspathines, Gobryas, Hydarnes, Megabyzus and Intaphrenes, and the six had just agreed to act against the Magus when Darius arrived from Persia. Darius told them that he had come for the very same purpose, and when the others hesitated, he warned them that delay was dangerous and that one traitor could ruin them all. They decided to strike that same day, and they went to the palace together.

The seven passed the guards easily because of their rank, and in the inner rooms they found the two Magi, the false king and his brother, who had helped to deceive the Persians. There was a short and confused struggle in a darkened room, and two of the conspirators were wounded, but the impostor was killed. Furious at the deception, the people killed every Magus they could find, and Herodotus says that on the festival of that day no Magus dares to appear in public.

When the trouble had passed, the seven nobles debated what sort of government Persia ought to have, and Herodotus tells us that the speeches were made, although some of the Greeks refused to believe it. Otanes argued that power should be shared by all citizens, Megabyzus preferred rule by a few of the best men, and Darius declared that nothing could be better than one excellent ruler. Four of the seven voted for a king, and Otanes then asked only that neither he nor his descendants should ever be ruled by anybody.

The nobles agreed to meet at sunrise outside the city, and to make king the man whose horse was the first to neigh. Darius told his groom Oebares of the plan, and Oebares led his master's stallion at night to the place where the horses would meet and brought him together with a mare that he loved. When the nobles reached the spot at dawn, the horse of Darius recognised the place and neighed, and a flash of lightning followed from a clear sky, which the others took as a sign.

The other six jumped from their horses and bowed to Darius, who became king in 522 BC and set about securing his rule. Soon afterwards he twisted his ankle so badly in a fall from his horse that he could not sleep, and the Egyptian doctors, who were thought the best in the world, made it worse. A Greek slave named Democedes, a doctor from Croton, was brought before him in chains and cured the king with gentle treatment, and Darius rewarded him with two pairs of golden fetters.

Under Cyrus and Cambyses, the subject peoples had simply made gifts to the king, but Darius divided the empire into twenty provinces and gave each one a governor, whom the Persians called a satrap. Each province paid a fixed tax, in silver or in the produce of the land, and Herodotus lists them one by one, noting that India, the farthest east, paid in gold dust. The Persians said that Cambyses had been a master, Cyrus a father, and Darius a shopkeeper, because he made a profit out of everything.

The Royal Road, which ran from Sardis in the west to Susa in the east, had a hundred and eleven stations, and Herodotus judged that a traveller on foot needed about three months to complete it. Along the whole road the king kept stations with fresh men and horses, so that a message was passed from rider to rider, and Herodotus declares that nothing mortal travels faster. Neither snow nor rain nor heat nor darkness, he adds in a famous line, stopped these couriers from finishing their stage as quickly as possible.

Darius, who had observed how peoples differ, called some Greeks before him and asked what price would persuade them to eat the bodies of their dead fathers, and they replied that no sum on earth could do so. He then asked some Callatian Indians, who ate their dead out of piety, what would persuade them to burn their fathers as the Greeks did, and they begged him not to speak of such horrors. Herodotus concluded that custom is king of all, a line that he borrowed from the poet Pindar.

Darius decided to punish the Scythians, a people of horsemen who had once swept into Asia and had ruled the Medes for many years. The Scythians told Herodotus that they were the youngest of all nations, and that their first king, Targitaus, had been the son of Zeus and a daughter of the river Borysthenes. In his day, they said, a plough, a yoke, an axe and a drinking cup, all of gold, fell from the sky, and the kings of Scythia guarded this treasure with the greatest care.

The Scythians, Herodotus explains, had neither cities nor walls nor farms to defend, and they carried their houses with them in wagons and lived on the milk and meat of their herds. Since they were all excellent horsemen and archers, they could always keep clear of an enemy who tried to attack them, and no army could take their homes because they had none to be taken. He also describes their steam baths, in which they threw hemp seeds on hot stones and howled with pleasure at the vapour.

Darius crossed from Asia to Europe on a bridge built at the Bosporus by Mandrocles of Samos, a Greek engineer who was richly rewarded and who painted a picture of the crossing as an offering to the goddess Hera. At the river Danube, which Herodotus calls the Ister, the Ionian Greeks of his fleet formed a bridge of boats. Darius tied sixty knots in a strap and ordered them to untie one each day and guard the bridge until they were gone, after which they might sail home.

As the Persians advanced, a messenger arrived from the Scythians, laid down a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows, and left without a word. Darius supposed that this was a gift of surrender, since the mouse stood for the earth, the frog for the water, the bird for the sky and the arrows for the Scythians' weapons. Gobryas, however, who was one of the seven, read the message rather differently: unless the Persians could fly like birds, burrow like mice or leap into the marshes like frogs, they would be shot with arrows and never go home.

The Scythians withdrew before the Persians, driving their cattle ahead of them, burying the wells and the springs, and leading the invaders deeper and deeper into the empty plains. Darius sent to their king Idanthyrsus, urging him either to fight or to submit, and the king answered that he had no cities or crops to lose and would fight only when it suited him. As for masters, he added, the Scythians acknowledged only Zeus, and in place of earth and water, Darius should expect to receive arrows.

At last the Scythians seemed ready to give battle, and the two armies drew up in lines facing each other, but just then a hare sprang out from the ground between them and ran across the field. The Scythians dropped their formation and rushed after it with cries of excitement, and Darius, when he asked what the noise meant, learned that they were hunting. He turned to his officers and remarked that these men held the Persians in great contempt, and that he now saw that they would be very difficult to defeat.

At last Darius lit his camp fires and slipped away in the night, leaving behind the sick men and the donkeys, whose braying kept the Scythians busy for a time. The Scythians raced to the Danube bridge to urge the Ionian Greeks to break it down and go home, and Miltiades of Athens argued that they should do so. Histiaeus of Miletus replied that every one of them owed his power to Darius, and the other tyrants agreed, so the bridge was kept, and the Persians returned to Asia in about 513 BC.

From Scythia, Herodotus turns to Libya, as the Greeks called Africa, and records the strange story of the Nasamonians, a desert people. Five of their young men, chosen by lot, set out to cross the great sandy waste, and after many days they came upon fruit trees and began to eat. There a band of small dark men seized them and led them across marshes to a city beside a great river full of crocodiles, perhaps the Niger, though nobody knows for certain.

Herodotus also reports that King Necho of Egypt, about 600 BC, sent Phoenician sailors down the Red Sea with orders to sail round Africa and return by the Mediterranean. Each autumn they landed, sowed some grain and waited for the harvest, and in the third year they came home through the Pillars of Heracles. They said that as they sailed west around the southern tip, they had the sun on their right hand, which Herodotus could not believe, though it is just what would be seen south of the equator.

Darius was eager to learn where the great river Indus reached the sea, and so he sent a Greek captain named Scylax, of Caryanda, to sail down the river and then westward along the coast. Scylax and his men reached Egypt after thirty months, and Herodotus says that after the voyage Darius conquered the Indians and made use of the sea. By this time the Persian Empire reached from the Danube and the Nile in the west to the Indus in the east.

After Peisistratus, Athens was ruled as a tyranny by his sons Hippias and Hipparchus. In 514 BC two friends named Harmodius and Aristogeiton killed Hipparchus during a festival and were themselves killed. Hippias, who now trusted nobody, ruled for four more years with a much heavier hand, and the Athenians began to long for their freedom.

The Alcmaeonids, an Athenian family in exile, had been hired to rebuild the temple at Delphi, and they used marble for the front when the contract only called for stone. Whenever Spartans came to consult the oracle, the priestess, who was said to have been persuaded, told them that they must free Athens, and the Spartans, though they were friends of the tyrants, obeyed the god. After one failed attempt, a second Spartan army marched north in 510 BC, and Hippias was forced to leave Athens with his family and go into exile in Asia.

Cleisthenes, an Alcmaeonid who won the people to his side, reorganised Athens into ten new tribes so that every citizen had a share in the government, and a rival of his was soon defeated. Herodotus remarks that the Athenians, who had been no better than their neighbours under tyrants, became the strongest of all once they were free, because each man worked for himself rather than for a master. It is one of the earliest descriptions that survives of the system we now call democracy, and its lesson seems to have been learned quickly.

Aristagoras, the ruler of Miletus, came to Sparta to beg King Cleomenes to help the Ionian Greeks against Persia, and he brought with him a bronze tablet on which the whole world was engraved. When Cleomenes learned that the Persian king lived three months' journey inland, he ordered the visitor to leave Sparta before sunset, for no Spartan would lead an army so far from the sea. Aristagoras tried to bribe him, but the king's young daughter Gorgo cried out that her father had better go before the stranger corrupted him.

Aristagoras then went to Athens, where he told the assembly that the Persians were weak and that the Greeks of Asia were their own kin. It struck Herodotus that it proved easier to deceive thirty thousand Athenians than a single Spartan king, for the people voted to send twenty ships, and the city of Eretria added five more. These vessels, he says, were the beginning of evils for Greeks and for foreigners alike.

Histiaeus, the former ruler of Miletus, was kept at the court of Darius under the pretext of friendship, and from Susa he longed to be sent home. Because the roads were watched, he shaved the head of his most trusted slave, wrote a message on his scalp, and waited until the hair had grown before sending him to Aristagoras with instructions to shave it again. The message told Aristagoras to revolt against Persia, and it was in this strange way that the Ionian revolt of 499 BC began.

Aristagoras saw that the Ionians would follow him only if he offered them freedom, and so he gave up his own position as ruler, declared that Miletus would be a free city, and encouraged the other cities to do likewise. They threw out the tyrants whom Persia had set over them, some of whom were handed over to their own citizens, and the revolt quickly spread along the whole coast. The Ionians understood that the fight was dangerous, but they hoped that the help of Athens and Eretria would be enough.

In 498 BC the Greeks marched inland to Sardis, which they took, though the citadel held out. Since the houses of the city had roofs of reed, a single house that caught fire spread the flames across the whole town, and the great temple of the goddess Cybele burned with it. The Persians later used the burning of this temple as an excuse to burn Greek temples in their turn, and the Greeks, hearing that the Persians were gathering, retreated to the coast.

When the news reached Darius, he was less concerned about the Ionians, whom he knew he would punish, than about the Athenians, and he asked who they might be. On being told, he took his bow, shot an arrow high into the sky, and prayed that Zeus would allow him to take revenge on Athens. Then he appointed a servant to say to him three times at every dinner that he should remember the Athenians.

The Persian forces caught the retreating Greeks near Ephesus and defeated them, killing many, including a famous champion of Eretria. The Athenians, who had taken a long journey for a short and unlucky adventure, went home and refused every plea from Aristagoras to return. The revolt, however, did not die, because it spread to Cyprus and the Hellespont, and the Persians had to fight on several fronts at once.

By 494 BC, the Persians had recovered Cyprus and several of the rebel cities, and they gathered a huge army and a fleet, mostly of Phoenician ships, to crush Miletus. The Ionians decided not to meet the army in the field but to defend the city from the sea, and they assembled their ships off the little island of Lade. They had three hundred and fifty-three ships, according to Herodotus, and they seemed to have a real chance of resisting.

Dionysius of Phocaea, a skilled seaman, took command of the Ionian fleet and drilled the crews daily, but after a week they complained that the work was more than they could stand. Some of their leaders had already made secret agreements with the Persians, and when the battle began at Lade, the Samians raised their sails and left the line. The remaining Greek ships fought bravely, especially those of Chios, but the battle was lost.

Miletus, the first city of the revolt, was besieged and taken in 494 BC, and most of the men were killed and the women and children carried off as slaves. When the Athenian writer Phrynichus produced a tragedy about the fall of the city, the whole audience burst into tears, and the Athenians fined him a thousand drachmas for reminding them of a sorrow so close to their own. They also forbade anyone to perform the play again, so that the work which had moved them so deeply was lost from the stage.

After the revolt, the Persian governor Artaphernes took sensible steps to prevent another one, by making the Ionian cities agree to settle their quarrels in court instead of raiding each other. He also had their lands measured and fixed the tribute that each city should pay, which was not very different from the sum they paid before. Herodotus adds that Mardonius removed the tyrants and set up democracies in the Ionian cities, which he says should surprise any Greek who refused to believe that the Persians had discussed democracy.

In 492 BC Mardonius led a large Persian army and fleet along the northern coast of the Aegean toward Greece, but his ships rounded the cape of Mount Athos just as a great north wind arose. The storm threw the vessels against the rocks and drowned so many of the crews that Herodotus puts the losses at about three hundred ships and twenty thousand men. Some of the men were carried off by the sea, and others died of cold, and Mardonius, who was also wounded in a night attack on land, returned to Asia.

In the following year, Darius sent heralds to the Greek cities to ask for earth and water, the traditional signs of submission, and many of the islands and cities did as he asked, including the island of Aegina. At Athens the heralds were thrown into a pit, and at Sparta they were thrown into a well and told to fetch their earth and water from the bottom. By these two acts, the two leading cities of Greece declared that they would not submit, and Darius resolved to attack them both.

Miltiades, the son of Cimon, was an Athenian who had ruled the Chersonese for years as a vassal of Persia, and who had urged the Ionians to break the bridge on the Danube during Darius's Scythian war. When the Phoenician fleet drew near in 493 BC, he escaped to Athens with a few ships, and his enemies accused him of being a tyrant, but the people acquitted him. He knew the Persians better than any other Greek, and they elected him one of their ten generals.

In the spring of 490 BC, the Persian army, which had been gathered in Cilicia, sailed across the Aegean under the command of Datis and Artaphernes, with Hippias as their guide. At the holy island of Delos, where the Greeks believed that Apollo and Artemis had been born, Datis refused to land with his soldiers and burned three hundred talents of frankincense on the altar. Herodotus adds that Delos shook with an earthquake soon after the fleet left, which the Delians took as a sign of troubles to come.

The Persians landed on the island of Euboea and besieged Eretria, whose citizens had sent help to the Ionians, and for six days they fought off every assault. On the seventh, two leading men betrayed the city, and the Persians burned the temples in revenge for the temples burned at Sardis. They then carried the people away as captives to the interior of Persia, where Darius settled them in a village and treated them kindly.

Hippias, who advised the Persians that Marathon was a good place to land because it was suited to cavalry and close to Athens, guided the fleet there from Eretria. While he marshalled the army on the shore, he was seized by a violent fit of sneezing and coughing, and one of his teeth fell out onto the sand where he could not find it. He said sadly that this land was not theirs and that they would never subdue it, since his tooth was all of it that he would ever possess.

Before the battle, the Athenians sent a runner named Pheidippides to Sparta to ask for help, and Herodotus says that he covered about two hundred and forty kilometres in two days. On the way, he reports, the god Pan appeared to Pheidippides and promised to aid Athens, a vision that the Athenians later honoured with a shrine. The Spartans received the message with sympathy but replied that religion forbade them to march before the moon was full.

At the camp near Marathon, the ten Athenian generals were divided, five wishing to fight and five fearing that they were too few to face such an army. Miltiades went to Callimachus, the war leader, whose vote could settle the question, and told him that it now lay in his power either to enslave Athens or to make her free. Callimachus, who had been moved by these words, cast his vote for battle, and the decision was made.

The small city of Plataea sent all its fighting men to join the Athenians, who had once helped them and who would never forget it. The generals who had voted for battle offered their days of command to Miltiades, who accepted them, but who waited for his own turn before launching the attack. He used the time to plan his line carefully, making his flanks strong and his centre thin, so that it would reach as far as the Persian line did.

When the day of Miltiades came, the Athenians drew up in line, with their flanks strong and their centre thin, and waited for the omens to prove favourable. Then they ran across the whole distance between the armies, about one and a half kilometres, and Herodotus says that no Greek army had ever charged in such a fashion. The Persians, seeing them come without cavalry or archers, believed that they had gone mad, and it was a bold plan which nearly failed.

The fighting was long, with the Persians breaking through the centre and pursuing the Athenians inland, while on the wings the Greeks drove their enemies back and then drew together to attack the Persians who had broken through. The invaders fled to their ships, and the Athenians followed them down the beach and captured seven vessels before the rest sailed away. Herodotus tells us that 192 Athenians fell that day and about 6,400 Persians, and that the Athenians put their dead under a great mound that still stands at Marathon.

The Athenian war leader, Callimachus, fell in the battle, and so did Stesilaus, one of the generals. Cynegirus, a brave Athenian, seized the stern of a Persian ship as it was putting out to sea, and lost his hand when it was struck off by an axe. Another man, Epizelus, was struck blind in the middle of the fight, although he had not been wounded, and he said afterwards that a huge armed man had appeared before him whose beard covered his whole shield.

As soon as the fighting ended, a shield was seen flashing a signal from a hill, and it was whispered that the family of the Alcmaeonids had given it to the Persians, though Herodotus refuses to believe the charge. The Persian fleet sailed round the cape of Sunium toward Athens in the hope of arriving before the army, but the Athenians hurried back the same day and camped in plain view of the ships. The Persians, finding that they were too late, turned around and sailed for Asia.

When the moon was full, two thousand Spartans marched out of their city and reached Attica in three days, so great was their haste. They had come too late for the battle, but they were still keen to see the Persians, and they went to Marathon and looked at the bodies. They praised the Athenians for what they had done, and then they went home.

After his victory, Miltiades persuaded the Athenians to give him seventy ships, promising to lead them to gold, but his real aim was to punish the island of Paros, which had helped the Persians. The siege failed, and Miltiades hurt his thigh badly as he fled, and when the Athenians heard that he had returned without money, they fined him fifty talents. The wound turned bad, and he died soon afterwards, and his son Cimon paid the fine.

When the news of Marathon reached Asia, Darius was enraged, and he began to raise a far larger army to punish the Greeks, spending three years in preparation. Then Egypt revolted, and before he could deal with it, Darius died in 486 BC after reigning for thirty-six years. His sons quarrelled over the succession, but with the advice of the exiled Spartan king Demaratus, the throne passed to Xerxes, who put down the revolt in Egypt and returned to the plans of his father.

Xerxes at first had no great wish to attack Greece, but his cousin Mardonius, who had been wounded at Athos and still longed to govern Greece, urged him on at every chance. He argued that the Athenians had wronged the Persians and had to be punished, and he praised Europe as a beautiful land whose trees were fit only for the king. Some of the Greeks who depended on Persian goodwill, in particular the powerful families of Thessaly, joined their voices to his.

Xerxes called his nobles together and declared that he would not be less than his forefathers, who had added land and power to Persia, and that he would bridge the Hellespont and burn Athens. Only his uncle Artabanus dared to oppose him, warning that Cyrus and Darius had both met disaster in distant wars and that the land and the sea would prove his greatest enemies. Xerxes replied furiously that Artabanus would be punished if he were not his father's brother.

After a sleepless night, Xerxes told the council that he had changed his mind, but that night a tall and handsome figure came to him in a dream. The figure warned him that if he did not march, he would be brought as low as quickly as he had been raised high, and the same dream came again the next night. Xerxes, frightened, ordered Artabanus to put on the royal robes and sleep in the royal bed, and the figure came to Artabanus as well, who was convinced that a god wished for the war.

For four years the king gathered soldiers, ships, and supplies from every part of his huge empire, and he ordered a great canal to be cut across the neck of land beside Mount Athos, where Mardonius had lost his fleet. Herodotus says that it would have been easy to drag the ships across the isthmus, and that the canal was dug only to show the king's power. The Phoenicians, who dug with sloping sides, finished their share, while the other workers, who cut straight walls, saw them collapse and had to dig again.

To carry his army into Europe, Xerxes ordered two bridges to be built across the Hellespont, one made by the Phoenicians with flax cables and one by the Egyptians with papyrus, but a violent storm wrecked them both. In his rage, the king ordered the sea to be given three hundred lashes and to have a pair of fetters thrown into it, and he put the engineers to death. Herodotus, who thought the punishment of the sea foolish and arrogant, adds that new engineers built two bridges of ships, one of three hundred and sixty and the other of three hundred and fourteen.

At Sardis the army was entertained by Pythius the Lydian, the richest man in the empire after the king, who offered to pay for the whole campaign out of his own wealth of nearly four million gold darics. The king was so delighted by the generosity that he refused the gift, made the sum up to four million with a few thousand coins of his own, and called him his guest-friend. As the army left Sardis, according to Herodotus, the sun darkened mysteriously in a clear sky, which the Persian priests took to be a sign that the Greeks would be defeated.

From a white marble throne on a hill at Abydos, Xerxes looked down at the Hellespont and saw the sea covered with his ships and the shore crowded with his men. At first he was glad, but then he wept, and he explained to Artabanus that he was thinking how short life is, since not one of all those men would be alive in a hundred years. Artabanus answered that life held even sadder things than its shortness, for men were often so wretched that they wished to die.

At dawn, the Persians burned incense on the bridges and strewed the roadway with myrtle, and as the sun rose, Xerxes poured wine from a golden cup into the sea and prayed that nothing might prevent him from conquering Europe. He then threw the cup, a golden bowl and a Persian sword into the Hellespont, and the army began to cross, which according to Herodotus took seven days and nights without a pause. A local man is said to have cried out to Zeus, asking why he had taken the shape of a Persian and the name of Xerxes in order to destroy Greece.

At Doriscus, on the coast of Thrace, Xerxes had his army counted by packing ten thousand men into a space, fencing it round, and filling it again and again. Herodotus says that this gave one million seven hundred thousand foot soldiers, and with the crews and camp followers he reckons the host at over five million, which no historian now believes. Most scholars think that the army was not nearly so large, although it was probably the biggest force that the Greeks had ever seen.

From a Sidonian ship, Xerxes reviewed his fleet of more than twelve hundred warships, which Herodotus lists by their nations, with the Phoenicians, Egyptians, Cypriots and Ionians among them. Of all the captains, the historian says that he will name only Artemisia, queen of his own city of Halicarnassus, who commanded five ships and whose were the most famous in the fleet after those of Sidon. She had joined the war although she could have stayed at home, and Xerxes valued her advice above that of all his other allies.

The Greek cities that were willing to resist met at the Isthmus of Corinth, settled their quarrels, and swore to work together, with Sparta taking the lead on land and sea. They sent envoys to Argos, Crete, Corcyra and Syracuse, and Gelon, the ruler of Syracuse, offered an enormous army and two hundred ships on the condition that he should command all of them. The Spartans replied that their ancestors would groan to hear that Sparta had given up the leadership, and the Athenians refused to hand over the fleet.

A little earlier, the Athenians had struck a rich vein of silver at Laurium, and it had been planned to give each citizen ten drachmas from the profits. Themistocles, a man of great energy and foresight, persuaded them to spend the money on two hundred warships, using the war with the nearby island of Aegina as his excuse. Herodotus says that the ships were never used against Aegina, but that they saved Greece when the Persians came.

The Athenians asked the oracle what to do, and the priestess first answered that they should flee to the ends of the earth, because their city would be destroyed. When they begged for a better answer, she said that a wall of wood would save them, and that divine Salamis would destroy the children of women. Some thought the wall meant the thorn fence around the Acropolis, but Themistocles argued that the oracle would not call Salamis divine if Greeks were to die there, so the wall had to mean the ships.

The Greeks sent three spies to Sardis, who were caught and condemned to death, but when Xerxes heard of it, he ordered his guards to take them around the whole camp, to show them his infantry and cavalry. Once they had seen everything and had satisfied their curiosity, they were to be sent home, and the king explained that killing them would not weaken the Greeks while their return would only frighten them. Herodotus does not say whether the news did frighten them, but the Greeks fought on.

After Sparta had killed the heralds of Darius, two noble Spartans, Sperthias and Bulis, volunteered to go to Persia and give themselves to Xerxes in payment for the crime. A Persian governor offered to make them important men in the empire, but they replied that he knew only slavery and had no idea of freedom, which they would defend with spears and with axes. Xerxes said that he would not do what the Spartans had done in violating the rights of heralds, and so he let them go.

A Greek army of ten thousand heavy infantry marched north to hold the narrow Vale of Tempe, but King Alexander of Macedon warned them that the Persians were too numerous and could use other passes. The Greeks, seeing the danger of being trapped, withdrew to the south, and the Thessalians, left without protection, made terms with Xerxes. It was clear that the defence of Greece would have to be made much farther south.

As the Persian army marched through Macedonia, Herodotus reports that lions came down from the hills at night and attacked the camels that carried the baggage, though they harmed no other animal and no man. Some of the rivers were drunk dry by the army, and the cities that had to feed it were ruined by the cost, for a single dinner for the king in the city of Thasos cost four hundred talents. A man of Abdera joked that the people should thank the gods, because the king did not eat twice in a day.

The Greeks decided to meet the Persians at places where the numbers of the enemy would count for little, namely at the narrow pass of Thermopylae by land and at the straits of Artemisium by sea. The Athenians supplied the largest share of the fleet, but they gave way and accepted the Spartan Eurybiades as commander, for they judged that a quarrel over leadership would be a greater danger than the enemy. Herodotus says that this generous act saved Greece, since a quarrel about leadership might have destroyed the whole alliance before it began.

The Spartans were then celebrating a religious festival and did not wish to send their whole army, so King Leonidas marched with a small advance guard of three hundred men, all of them chosen because they had living sons. The oracle at Delphi had told Sparta that either the city would be sacked by the Persians or a king of the house of Heracles would be killed. Herodotus suggests that Leonidas understood the message, and that he went to Thermopylae expecting to die, in order to save his city.

As Leonidas marched north, men from the cities of the Peloponnese joined him, among them soldiers from Tegea, Mantinea, Corinth and Mycenae, and in central Greece the Thespians, the Thebans and the Phocians came to swell his numbers. Herodotus lists each contingent, and it seems that there were about seven thousand Greeks in the pass when they were all gathered, as against the enormous host that was to come. They had been told that the main Greek army would follow, and many of them were expecting it.

When the Persian army camped within sight of Thermopylae, the Greeks in the pass began to quarrel, and the Peloponnesians urged that they should withdraw and hold the Isthmus of Corinth instead. The Phocians and Locrians, whose homes lay behind the pass, were furious at the idea of being abandoned, and Leonidas voted to stay where they were and to send messengers to every city asking for more troops. The Greeks repaired an old wall across the narrowest place and made ready to defend it.

Xerxes sent a rider to see what the Greeks were doing, and the scout reported that some of them were exercising while others combed their long hair. The king found this absurd, but Demaratus explained that it was the Spartan custom to dress their hair when they were about to risk their lives. He added that if Xerxes beat these men, no other people in the world would dare to raise a hand against him.

For four days Xerxes waited in the hope that the Greeks would flee, and on the fifth, losing patience, he ordered the Medes to attack and to bring the Greeks to him alive. Before the fight, a man is said to have warned a Spartan named Dieneces that the Persian arrows were so numerous that they hid the sun. Dieneces replied cheerfully that this was good news, for it meant that they would be able to fight in the shade.

In the narrow ground the numbers of the Persians were of no use, and the Medes were cut down in great numbers by the longer spears of the Greeks. On the second day, Xerxes sent in the Immortals, his best soldiers, but they fared no better, and the Spartans fought in careful order, sometimes pretending to run away and then turning on the pursuers. Herodotus tells us that the king sprang three times from his throne in fear for his army.

Then a local man named Ephialtes, hoping to earn a reward from the Persian king, revealed that a goat-track climbed over the mountain and descended behind the Greek position. Xerxes sent the Immortals along it under Hydarnes, and at dawn they surprised the thousand Phocians guarding the summit, who fled to a hilltop, supposing that they themselves were the target. Hydarnes, who wished only to descend, ignored them and hurried down the mountain, and Herodotus adds bluntly that Ephialtes is remembered in Greece as a traitor to this day.

That night the seer Megistias examined the sacrifice and told the Greeks that death would come at dawn, and deserters from the Persian camp soon brought word that the Immortals were marching round the mountain. At first light, the scouts from the heights ran in to say the same, and the Greek commanders held a hurried council in which opinions were divided. Some wished to hold their positions and others to retreat, and Leonidas listened to every opinion before he made his own decision known.

Leonidas saw that the allies were uneasy, and he told most of them to depart, so that they might be saved to fight another day. The Spartans, who were bound by their laws never to retreat, remained, and Herodotus believes that Leonidas also wished to win glory for Sparta, and to fulfil the oracle that had spoken of a king's death. The seven hundred Thespians refused to leave the Spartans, and four hundred Thebans stayed against their will.

Knowing that this was the last day, the Greeks advanced into the wider part of the pass and fought with desperate courage, killing great numbers of Persians while the officers drove their men forward with whips. When the Greek spears were broken, they fought with swords, and Leonidas fell, and a savage struggle began for his body, in which the Greeks drove the enemy back four times before they dragged the king away. Herodotus says that two brothers of Xerxes were killed in this fight, and that the Persians lost many men in the narrow ground.

When the Immortals appeared at their rear, the Greeks drew back to a small hill behind the wall and made a last stand together, while the Thebans, separating from them, held out their hands and surrendered. Those who remained fought on with their swords, if they still had them, and with their hands and teeth, until the Persians overwhelmed them with a storm of arrows. On that hill the Greeks later set up a stone, and its famous verse asks the passing stranger to tell the Spartans that their men lie there, obedient to their orders.

Eurytus and Aristodemus, two of the three hundred, had been sent away with an eye illness, and Eurytus, hearing that the Persians had come round, had himself led back into the battle, where he died. Aristodemus did not do so, and he returned to Sparta, where no one would talk to him or light his fire, and he was given the nickname of the Trembler. Herodotus tells us that he washed away the shame two years later at Plataea, where he died fighting as no other Spartan did.

At Artemisium, the Greek captains wanted to sail away as soon as they saw the size of the Persian fleet, and the people of Euboea begged them to stay long enough to move their families. Themistocles accepted thirty talents from the Euboeans, gave five to the Spartan admiral Eurybiades and three to the Corinthian Adeimantus, and kept the rest for himself. The two commanders, who thought the money had come from Themistocles, agreed to stay.

As the Persian fleet lay at anchor off the coast of Magnesia, a violent storm from the east struck it and raged for three days, and the Persian priests tried to charm the wind with sacrifices and spells. Herodotus reports that about four hundred ships were lost, and the Athenians believed that Boreas, the north wind, who by legend was married to an Athenian princess, had come to their aid in answer to their prayers. A second squadron that had been sent round Euboea was wrecked in the same way.

For three days the Greek fleet fought the Persians in the straits of Artemisium, and though the battles were not decisive, the Greeks gave as good as they received, and many of their ships were damaged. When news of Thermopylae reached them, they sailed south, but Themistocles first had messages carved on stones beside the watering places, begging the Ionians in the Persian fleet to change sides or at least to fight badly. He hoped that if the Ionians did not obey, Xerxes might at least come to suspect them of treachery.

Xerxes toured the battlefield at Thermopylae, and a few deserters from Arcadia, who were poor and in need of work, came to his camp and told him that the Greeks were celebrating the Olympic Games. When asked what the prize was, they answered that it was a crown of olive leaves, and a Persian officer named Tigranes exclaimed to Mardonius that these were men who competed for honour rather than for money. Herodotus records the remark without comment, but it shows how strange the Greek love of honour seemed to men who served a king.

The people of Delphi, learning that the Persians were approaching, asked the oracle whether they should bury the treasures of the god, and the oracle replied that Apollo could protect his own. As the invaders drew near the temple of Athena Pronaia, thunderbolts fell from the sky and two great rocks tore away from Mount Parnassus and crushed many of them. The terrified Persians fled, and the Delphians, who said that they saw two giant armed men pursuing them, came down from the mountain and killed more.

As the Persians marched toward Attica, the Athenians proclaimed that every citizen should save his household as best he could, and the women, children and old people were sent to Troezen, Aegina and Salamis. Herodotus says that a great snake lived in the temple of Athena on the Acropolis and was given a honey cake every month. When the priestess reported that this month's cake had been left untouched, the citizens took it as a sign that Athena had already left her city, and they were all the readier to follow.

A small band of Athenians, who had believed that the wooden wall meant the fence of the Acropolis, barricaded themselves on the Acropolis and rolled great stones down upon the Persians as they climbed. The invaders found a steep and unguarded path on the north side, and some of the defenders threw themselves from the walls, while others took refuge in the temple. The Persians killed those whom they found there and set fire to the Acropolis, and Xerxes sent a rider to Susa with news of the capture of Athens.

On the day after the capture, Xerxes ordered the Athenian exiles with his army to go up to the Acropolis and offer sacrifice in the Athenian manner, perhaps because of a dream or out of remorse. When they reached the temple, they found that the sacred olive tree, which had been burned to the ground, had put out a new shoot a cubit long. The Athenians took this as a sign that their city would live again, and the story was told for centuries afterwards.

At a council on Salamis, the commanders from the Peloponnese argued that the fleet should withdraw to the Isthmus of Corinth, where it could fight beside the army. They said there was no sense in defending a city already taken, and when Themistocles rose to speak, Adeimantus of Corinth told him that at the games those who start too early are whipped. Themistocles answered calmly that those who are left behind at the starting post are never crowned, and then he made his case in earnest.

Themistocles then took the Spartan commander aside and argued that in the narrow waters off Salamis the Greeks would fight at an advantage, while in the open sea off the Isthmus their small fleet would be crushed. He added that if the allies did not stay, the Athenians, who had two hundred ships and who made up the bulk of the fleet, would take their families and sail away to found a new city in Italy. Eurybiades, who understood that without the Athenians there would be no fleet at all, agreed to stay and fight.

The Greek commanders argued far into the night, and since the Peloponnesians seemed likely to win the vote, Themistocles slipped out of the council and sent his trusted servant Sicinnus across the water to the Persian camp. The message claimed that the Athenian general was secretly on the king's side and that the Greeks were about to run away, and that if Xerxes attacked at once, he would find them in disarray and quarrelling. Themistocles knew that if the Greeks were shut in, they would have no choice but to fight.

Xerxes asked each of his commanders whether he should give battle at sea, and all of them advised it except Artemisia. She reminded him that the Greeks were as much better sailors than his men as men are than women, and urged him to wait, since the Greeks would soon run short of food and scatter. Xerxes praised her wisdom warmly, but he followed the view of the majority and gave the order to fight.

That night Aristides, a famous Athenian whom his fellow citizens had exiled and who was known as the Just, crossed over from Aegina in a small boat to find Themistocles, to whom he had always been an enemy. He proposed that they put their quarrel aside, and told him that the Persian ships had closed all the exits from the straits. Themistocles replied that it was his own work, and a deserting ship from Tenos soon proved that Aristides's news was right.

At dawn, Themistocles spoke to the assembled crews, setting what was noble against what was base, and bade them embark. The Greek ships backed away from the advancing enemy, as if to run aground, until an Athenian trireme under Ameinias shot forward and rammed the nearest Persian ship. The other Greeks, not wishing to be left behind, rowed in to join him, and the battle, which was fought in late September 480 BC, began in earnest.

In the narrow waters the huge Persian fleet could not manoeuvre, and when the leading ships were pushed back, those in the rear came on, so that the vessels fouled one another and were smashed by Greek rams. Xerxes watched from a golden throne on the slope of Mount Aigaleos, with scribes beside him who wrote down the names of captains who fought well or ill. The battle lasted all day, and the Persian losses were far heavier than those of the Greeks.

Queen Artemisia, whose ship was being pursued by an Athenian trireme, could not escape because other ships blocked the way, and she decided to ram one of the king's own allies, the ship of the Calyndians. The Athenian captain, supposing that she was a friend or that she had gone over to the Greeks, turned away, while Xerxes, who watched from the shore, thought that she had sunk an enemy ship. Herodotus says that Xerxes cried out that his men had become women and his women men, a remark that was long remembered in Greece.

By evening, the Persian fleet was in headlong flight toward Phalerum, while Aristides landed soldiers on the little island of Psyttaleia and destroyed the Persian troops posted there. The Greeks, who thought the enemy would renew the battle the next day, prepared for a second fight, though the Persians were in no state to do so. The battle of Salamis, one of the most decisive sea fights in history, had broken the strength of the Persian navy.

Xerxes, fearing that the Greeks might sail to the Hellespont and cut his bridges, accepted Mardonius's offer to stay and conquer Greece with three hundred thousand picked troops. The retreat was long and wretched, for the soldiers ate grass and bark when supplies ran short, and disease swept through the camp. At the Hellespont the bridges had been broken by a storm, so the army crossed in ships, and Xerxes returned to Sardis, his great expedition a failure.

After the battle, the Greek commanders met at the Isthmus to give prizes for the most valuable service, and each man wrote his own name first, but most of them put Themistocles second. Since no one was awarded the first place, the Spartans gave Eurybiades an olive wreath for his courage and Themistocles one for his wisdom, and they presented him with the finest chariot in Sparta. Three hundred picked horsemen escorted him to the border, and Herodotus says that he was the only man the Spartans ever honoured in this way.

In the spring of 479 BC, Mardonius sent King Alexander of Macedon to Athens with an offer to rebuild the city, to give the Athenians more land, and to let them govern themselves if they would make an alliance with Persia. The Spartans, who feared that Athens would accept, sent their own envoys, and the Athenians gave the same reply to both, that they would never make terms with Xerxes so long as the sun held its course. They said that the Greeks were bound together by blood, language, shrines and customs.

In the summer of 479 BC, Mardonius invaded Attica again, and the Athenians, who had waited in vain for help from the Peloponnese, abandoned their city a second time and crossed to Salamis. He repeated his offer of peace, which they once more refused, and they sent envoys to Sparta to complain that the Spartans had done nothing while the Persians occupied Athens. If help did not come soon, the envoys warned, the Athenians would be forced to make their own terms.

The Spartans, busy with the festival of Hyacinthus and with building a wall across the Isthmus, put off the Athenian envoys for ten days. Then Chileus of Tegea warned the ephors that no wall could protect the Peloponnese if Athens joined Persia, and they acted at once. That very night five thousand Spartans marched out under Pausanias, each with seven helots to carry his baggage, and when the envoys came to say they would wait no longer, they learned that the army had already gone.

The Greek army that gathered near Plataea included, according to Herodotus, about forty thousand heavy infantry from many cities, besides a great number of lightly armed men. The Spartan Pausanias held the supreme command, and when the Athenians and Tegeans quarrelled over the left wing, the Athenians recalled their deeds from Marathon, and the army decided in their favour. The soldiers then took up positions on the slopes of Mount Cithaeron and looked down on the Persian camp beside the river.

Herodotus tells of a feast given by a rich Theban named Attaginus, at which fifty Persians and fifty Thebans shared couches, and a Persian who sat beside a man of Orchomenus began to weep. He said that few of the Persians and their allies at Plataea would be alive in a short while, that many of them knew it, and that the bitterest pain among men is to have understanding and no power. The Greek, a man named Thersander of Orchomenus, repeated these words to many people, and Herodotus says that he heard them from Thersander himself.

The Persian cavalry, led by the brave Masistius on a splendid horse with a golden bridle, attacked the Greeks in the foothills, and for a time the Megarians were hard pressed until the Athenians came to their help. Masistius's horse was wounded, and he fell and was killed after a stubborn fight, because his armour, which was made of gold and covered by a purple tunic, protected him from the first blows. The Persians, who loved him, mourned for him by cutting their hair and the manes of their horses.

For eleven days the two armies sat facing one another, because the sacrifices of each side forbade attack. Meanwhile Mardonius's cavalry cut off a convoy of food coming through a pass and fouled the spring of Gargaphia, the main source of drinking water for the Greeks. One night Alexander of Macedon, a secret friend of Greece, rode to the Athenian lines to warn them of an attack, and as the Greeks' position grew worse, Pausanias decided to withdraw.

That night the Greeks began to withdraw, but Amompharetus, a Spartan officer, declared that he would not run from foreigners and bring shame on Sparta, and he would not move his men. Pausanias argued with him until dawn, and at last Amompharetus took up a large stone with both hands and set it at his general's feet, saying that this was his pebble of voting against flight. Pausanias had to leave him behind, and at daybreak he moved off, with the stubborn officer following very slowly.

At dawn Mardonius saw the Greek positions empty and the army moving away, and believing that they were running from him, he sent a message mocking the Spartans, who had boasted that they never fled from battle. He then ordered his army to pursue the Greeks, and the Persians, who ran forward in no order at all, came across the plain with shouts and the noise of horses. Pausanias sent to the Athenians for help, but the Persian cavalry cut them off, and the Spartans and Tegeans stood alone.

The Persians planted their wicker shields in the ground and fired arrows at the Spartans, who knelt behind their own shields and endured the storm, for the sacrifices were unfavourable. Many Spartans fell, and Pausanias, looking toward the temple of Hera, prayed to the goddess not to deceive the hopes of the Greeks. At that moment the Tegeans, who could stand no more, rushed forward, and the omens became favourable at once.

At the signal the Spartans charged, and the Persians, who grabbed their spears and broke them in their hands, fought with courage but lacked both armour and skill. Mardonius, who fought on a white horse among a thousand picked men, was killed by a stone thrown by a Spartan named Arimnestus, and the Persians fled into their wooden fort, which the Athenians stormed after the Tegeans entered it. Artabazus, who had commanded forty thousand men, had already run away and never stopped until he reached Byzantium.

After the battle, Pausanias found the splendid tent of Mardonius, hung with fabrics and full of gold and silver vessels, and ordered the Persian cooks to prepare the dinner that they had made for their master. He then told his own servants to prepare an ordinary Spartan meal and called the Greek generals to see the two tables set side by side. He laughed and told them that the Persians, who lived in such luxury, had come all this way to take away the poor bread of the Greeks.

After the battle, the Greeks divided the spoils of the Persian camp and set aside a tenth for the gods. With it they paid for a golden tripod on a bronze column of three twisted snakes, which was set up at Delphi, and the names of the cities that fought at Plataea were carved on it. The gold has long since vanished, but part of the bronze snakes still stands in Istanbul, where it was carried in the fourth century AD.

While the Greeks were winning on land, their fleet under the Spartan king Leotychides lay at Delos, where a Samian envoy named Hegesistratus begged the admirals to free the Ionian Greeks. The Ionians, he said, would rise against Persia as soon as they were helped, and the fleet sailed across the Aegean to Samos. The Persians, who dared not fight, had drawn up their ships on the beach at Mycale and built a stockade around them, and the Greeks landed beside the camp and prepared to attack.

As the Greeks formed up on the shore, a rumour spread through the ranks that the army in Boeotia had defeated Mardonius, and a herald's staff was found lying on the beach, which the soldiers took for a sign. Herodotus notes that the report was true, and that it arrived on the very day of the battle at Plataea, which he regarded as a clear mark of the gods' favour. Encouraged by the news, the Greeks advanced against the stockade, where the Persians waited behind a row of wicker shields.

The Athenians and Corinthians led the attack, and when the Persians were pressed back behind their wicker shields, many of the Ionian Greeks in the Persian army turned on their masters. The Persians fell back into the stockade, and the Greeks broke in after them and burned the ships. Mycale was the first time since the Ionian revolt that the Greeks had gone on the attack in Asia, and for the Ionians it was a great moment of hope.

After the victory at Mycale, the Peloponnesian commanders proposed to move the Ionians to Europe and give them the lands of Greek cities that had sided with Persia, believing that Ionia could never be defended. The Athenians objected that the Ionians were their own colonists, and that it was not for the Peloponnesians to decide their fate, and the Spartans gave way. The Samians, Chians, Lesbians and other islanders were then admitted to the alliance and swore an oath never to desert it.

The Greek fleet sailed to the Hellespont, intending to break the bridges of Xerxes, and found them already ruined, so that the Spartans and their allies went home. The Athenians, under Xanthippus, stayed to besiege Sestos, held by Artayctes, who had plundered the shrine of the hero Protesilaus, and the starving Persians ate the straps of their beds. When the city fell, Artayctes was caught, and Herodotus says that a salted fish leaped in a guard's pan as a sign from Protesilaus, after which the governor was put to death.

Before leaving the Hellespont, the Athenians loaded onto their ships the great cables of the bridge that Xerxes had built, and they carried them home to be dedicated in the temples as a memorial of the war. With the departure of the fleet, the great Persian invasion of Greece was finally over, and Herodotus chose this moment to end the main part of his story. It was an end that fitted his subject well, for the tyrant's bridge had become a trophy.

Looking back over the long story, one may discern the lesson that Herodotus announced in his opening lines, that human prosperity never abides in one place and that the mighty of one age become the humble of the next. Solon had said as much to Croesus at Sardis, and Croesus later told Cyrus that human affairs are a wheel which, as it turns, does not permit the same men always to flourish. Persia had swallowed Lydia, Media, Babylon and Egypt, yet it had been turned back by a handful of small cities of free men.

Herodotus closes his great work with a story about Cyrus, set long before the invasion of Greece, when the Persians were still poor and rough hill people. When some of them proposed that they should leave their harsh land for a softer one, Cyrus replied that they were free to do so, but that soft countries breed soft men. He added that it was better to rule from a rugged country than to be slaves in a rich one, and the Persians chose to stay where they were.
